Tabsdata is a distributed, horizontally scalable system that runs on Kubernetes and can be deployed across a variety of Kubernetes providers. Tabsdata is organized into two conceptual layers: a resource layer and an execution layer. The resource layer consists of objects that users create to establish the structure of a Tabsdata workflow. These include objects like Tables and Functions, which determine when a workflow runs, what data flows through it, and what work is applied to that data. The execution layer consists of objects that Tabsdata creates when it reads and acts on resources from the resource layer. These objects make up the running workflow that performs work on data. This includes objects like Execution Plans, Transactions, and Function Runs. Server? Projects? Resource layer Groups? Collections? Functions? Connections? Tables? Execution layer Execution Plan? Functions are Tabsdata's unit of work. A function performs a single discrete step of moving data between external systems and internal Tabsdata Tables. There are three types of Tabsdata Functions: A publisher reads from an external system and writes into Tabsdata tables. A transformer reads from Tabsdata tables and writes into new Tabsdata tables. A subscriber reads from Tabsdata tables and writes out to an external system. A unique feature of Tabsdata is that it has its own internal storage for all data produced by functions. Tabsdata tables persistently store the data produced by functions. Every successful function run that returns data creates a new table version that sits alongside all previous versions of the table. persons Tabsdata›Collections›input›persons SchemaSample Schema Table schema defines the structure of a table by listing its columns and their data types. Object Type first_name str last_name str age i64 nationality str city str v2v1version While Tabsdata tables share some similarities to database tables, they also have some key differences. Rather than requiring a predefined schema, each version inside a table carries its own, allowing a table's schema to evolve across versions. This not only makes Tabsdata resilient to schema drift, but also stores a lineage of the table's evolution for observability and debugging. Table version history is available not only to users for viewing, but also to functions for ingestion. Functions can read historical table versions for use cases that require comparing historical data with incoming data.

Functions and tables declare how data should be moved. Tabsdata's reads these and builds the actual workflow that ingests, transforms, and loads your data.

Traditionally, as more steps are added to a data integration workflow, the more complex it is to orchestrate it. Tabsdata does not have this issue. Function are declarative and declare their own dependencies. Any functions that write to tables used by other functions are upstream dependent to them. Any functions that use tables produced by other functions are downstream dependent to them. When a Function is triggered, Tabsdata identifies its downstream dependencies and automatically builds an Execution Plan, a DAG (directed acytclic graph) that finds and executes all downstream dependencies. Compute and storage are independently scalable. Each Function runs as an isolated process within the Server's Kubernetes cluster. Storage can be distributed across local file storage or cloud storage providers such as Amazon S3, Azure Blob Storage, and Google Cloud Storage.

Authorization uses a direct permission model, where permissions are assigned directly to users rather than through roles. Credentials are stored separately from Functions in a secure credential store. This includes both Tabsdata's internal credentials and the credentials used by Connections to authenticate with external systems. note Even when credentials are provided inline through the CLI, Tabsdata automatically extracts and stores them in the credential store.

Tabsdata runs on Linux for production and macOS or Windows for development. A Collection is an organizational layer inside of a group that stores tables and functions. Collections help manage credentials for functions and define transaction boundaries for tables.

A Function is responsible for moving, and sometimes transforming, data from one place to another. Publishers and Subscribers that read from or write data to external systems also need a way to securely access sensitive credentials for those systems. Instead of hardcoding credentials directly into Function logic, Tabsdata abstracts credential management into a separate resource called a Connection. A Connection is defined in a .yaml file and bound to a Collection. Any Function registered to the same Collection can access those credentials at runtime. This allows users to store their credentials once and then securely provision those credentials to as many functions that need them. Learn more about connections here.

Triggering a Tabsdata Function creates an Execution Plan that executes the triggering Function along with any functions downstream dependent to it. Because an Execution Plan can span multiple Functions, Tabsdata needs to determine which data should be committed or rolled back if the Execution Plan fails partway through. Collections act as transaction boundaries within an Execution Plan. Tabsdata treats each participating Collection as a separate transaction and commits data to its Tables only when all participating Functions within that Collection complete successfully. If a Function within the transaction fails, Tabsdata rolls back all changes made to Tables within that transaction.

After creating a Collection, users can register Functions into that collection. If a collection is created inside the sources or destinations group, it can only store publisher or subscriber functions respectively and requires a connection to be bound Deleting a Collection removes the Collection and the resources it contains without affecting other Collections in the Project. See Create a Collection, Update a Collection, and Delete a Collection for step-by-step instructions.

A Connection is a resource that stores the credentials required to access an external system. Publisher and Subscriber Functions need credentials to connect to external systems to read and write data, but they do not store these sensitive credentials directly in their code. Instead, that configuration is defined in a Connection. Connections are .yaml files that contain relevant credentials and are attached to Collections, allowing all functions in that collection to access the required credentials during execution.

Connections are defined using .yaml files. The fields in a Connection depend on the external system and Connection type. For example, an S3 Connection stores the bucket, region, and credentials needed to access files in an S3 bucket. conn-s3.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.s3:S3SrcConn spec: bucket: 'acme-ingest' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: '$secret:AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID' secret_access_key: '$secret:AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY' bucket:strrequired region:strrequired credentials:AwsAccessSecretKeyrequired base_path:stroptional

Connections are bound to Publisher and Subscriber Collections. A Publisher Collection binds a Publisher to an input Connection. The Publisher defines what data to read from the external system and what Tables to create in Tabsdata, while the Connection provides the configuration and credentials needed to access that system during the Publisher's execution. A Subscriber Collection binds a Subscriber to an output Connection. The Subscriber defines which Tabsdata Tables to read and what data to write, while the Connection provides the configuration and credentials needed to access the destination system during the Subscriber's execution.

When configuring a connection , a credential can be passed directly as secret:<value>, or as a reference to an environment variable, written as $secret:<VARIABLE NAME>. Regardless of the method used, when the connection file is registered into Tabsdata, Tabsdata dehydrates the document by extracting any secrets into a separate secret store and storing a reference to the secret in the file. note For security, once credentials are stored in Tabsdata, they can only be accessed by a Tabsdata Function at runtime.

The S3Dest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Amazon S3.

The S3Src connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Amazon S3 into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a AwsAccessSecretKey connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Publisher connection, at the end of this page.

The bucket exists and is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The AWS principal can list the bucket and read every object matched by paths. The object format and compression match format and format_cfg.

Configure S3Src as the source of a publisher function to select the files that Tabsdata reads from S3. publish_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Src, SrcFileFormat @publisher( source=S3Src( paths=[ "incoming/orders.parquet", ], ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders): return orders paths:list[str]required format:SrcFileFormatoptional format_cfg:dictoptional initial_last_modified:datetimeoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

paths​ Defines the files that the publisher reads from S3. Each path is relative to the base_path configured in S3SrcConn. Source paths: cannot begin or end with / cannot contain empty path segments can contain a * glob in the final path segment For example: S3Src( paths=[ "orders/2026/*.parquet", "customers/customers.csv", ] ) Each element in paths represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function. When a path uses a glob to match multiple files, the matching files are provided through the corresponding publisher input. format​ Sets the format used to read the source files. Supported formats are AUTO, CSV, JSON, AVRO, PARQUET, and LOG. The default is AUTO, which determines the format from the file extension. format_cfg​ Sets format-specific reader options. Configuration is keyed by SrcFileFormat. initial_last_modified​ Sets the initial cutoff for incremental ingestion. On the first run, Tabsdata imports files modified at or after the specified timestamp. The cutoff then advances so subsequent runs only import newer files. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. The following options are supported: Option Description tabsdata.file.chunk_size Controls the size of chunks used when reading files. tabsdata.src_metadata.drop When True, excludes the @td.file.path metadata column. By default, rows read from S3 include a @td.file.path metadata column containing the s3:// URI of the file the row was read from.

The S3Dest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Amazon S3. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a AwsAccessSecretKey connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Subscriber connection, at the end of this page.
The bucket exists and is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The AWS principal can write objects under the configured base_path. The destination path is relative and does not contain a glob.

Configure S3Dest as the destination of a subscriber function to define where Tabsdata writes files in S3. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.s3 import S3Dest, DestFileFormat @subscriber( destination=S3Dest( paths=[ "exports/orders.parquet", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders paths:list[str]required format:DestFileFormatoptional format_cfg:dictoptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

paths​ Defines where the subscriber writes files in S3. Each path is relative to the base_path configured in S3DestConn. Destination paths: cannot begin or end with / cannot contain empty path segments cannot contain globs Each element in paths represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Destination paths can contain variables that Tabsdata substitutes when the subscriber runs: Variable Value ${EXEC_PLAN_ID} Current execution plan ID. ${TRX_ID} Current transaction ID. ${EXEC_PLAN_TS} Timestamp when the execution plan started. For example: S3Dest( paths=[ "exports/${EXEC_PLAN_ID}/orders.parquet", ] ) Dynamic paths can be used to create a new S3 object for each execution instead of overwriting an existing object. format​ Sets the format used to write the destination file. Supported formats are AUTO, CSV, JSON, AVRO, and PARQUET. The default is AUTO, which determines the format from the destination file extension. format_cfg​ Sets format-specific writer options. Configuration is keyed by DestFileFormat. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration. The tabsdata.file.chunk_size option controls the size of chunks used when writing files.

Each entry in a publisher's paths is one source slot. A literal path reads one object; a final-segment * glob can read several. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. initial_last_modified sets the cutoff for the first run. After a successful run, Tabsdata advances the cutoff so the same unchanged objects are not published again. Each entry in a subscriber's paths is one destination slot and maps by position to a returned value. Use ${EXEC_PLAN_ID}, ${TRX_ID}, or ${EXEC_PLAN_TS} in a path when every run needs a new object. A fixed path writes to the same location again.

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set trigger_by to change when the function runs. Tabsdata validates the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not contact Amazon S3 then. A bad path, credential, or permission fails when the function runs. Globs are allowed only for publisher source paths, and only in the final path segment. Subscriber destination paths cannot contain globs. All configured paths are relative to the connection's base_path.

Configure DatabricksSrc as the source of a publisher function to select the queries that Tabsdata runs against Databricks. publish_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher from tabsdatak.conn.databricks import DatabricksSrc @publisher( source=DatabricksSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM main.default.orders", ], ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders): return orders queries:list[str]required initial_values:dictoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

On later runs each parameter takes the value the publisher stored with ctx.set_attr(name, value), so a query can read only the rows added since the last run. For example: from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.databricks import DatabricksSrc @publisher( source=DatabricksSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM main.default.orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id"], initial_values={"last_id": 0}, ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> TableFrameSpec: row = orders.max_for("id") if row is not None and row["id"] is not None: ctx.set_attr("last_id", int(row["id"])) return orders src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration.

tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in Databricks. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Destination table names can be fully qualified or completed from the connection's catalog/schema defaults. if_table_exists​ "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and requires a merge_cfg list. See Merge configuration for a complete example. Controls what happens when the destination table already exists. "append" (the default) adds rows. "replace" overwrites the table. schema_evolution​ Controls how new columns in the returned frame are handled. "update" forwards mergeSchema=true to COPY INTO so new columns are added. "strict" is the default and leaves existing data columns unchanged. See Merging into SQL destinations for merge-specific behavior. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration.

Each entry in queries produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. For incremental reads, put named parameters such as :last_id in a query, set their first values with initial_values, and save the next values with ctx.set_attr() after a successful run.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a returned value. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" adds rows, "replace" overwrites the table, and "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key. With schema_evolution="update", append-style writes can add columns; "strict" does not change existing data columns.

Publisher queries and subscriber writes use the configured SQL warehouse. The Unity Catalog volume is the staging area used to move data. One- and two-part table names use the connection's catalog and schema defaults. Fully qualified names override them. Tabsdata does not contact the workspace when the collection is created. Workspace, token, warehouse, volume, and permission errors appear when the function runs.

The Db2 connector lets Tabsdata run queries against Db2 and write tables into Db2. The Db2Src connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Db2 into a Tabsdata table. The Db2Dest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Db2.

The Db2Src connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Db2 into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a Db2SrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Publisher connection, at the end of this page.
The Db2 server is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The connection user can run every query in queries and read every referenced table or view.

Configure Db2Src as the source of a publisher function to select the queries that Tabsdata runs against Db2. publish_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2Src @publisher( source=Db2Src( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM orders", ], ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders): return orders queries:list[str]required initial_values:dictoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

queries​ Defines the SQL queries the publisher runs against Db2. Each element in queries represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function. For example: Db2Src( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM country", "SELECT * FROM city", ], ) initial_values​ The first-run values for named parameters in queries, written :name. On later runs each parameter takes the value the publisher stored with ctx.set_attr(name, value), so a query can read only the rows added since the last run. Db2 folds unquoted identifiers to uppercase, so the column read back is ID. Parameters bind values such as IDs and timestamps, not identifiers. Schema and table names have to be written into the query. For example: from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2Src @publisher( source=Db2Src( queries=["SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id"], initial_values={"last_id": 0}, ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> TableFrameSpec: row = orders.max_for("ID") if row is not None and row["ID"] is not None: ctx.set_attr("last_id", int(row["ID"])) return orders src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration.

The Db2Dest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Db2. The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a Db2DestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Subscriber connection, at the end of this page.
The Db2 server is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The connection user can create missing destination tables and insert rows. With if_table_exists="replace", it can also truncate existing tables.

Configure Db2Dest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in Db2. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2Dest @subscriber( destination=Db2Dest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:stroptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in Db2. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. For example: Db2Dest( tables=[ "vendors", "items", ], ) if_table_exists​ Controls what happens when the destination table already has rows. "append" (the default) keeps inserting into the existing rows. "replace" truncates the table before inserting. Neither mode changes the destination table's schema, so the returned frame's columns need to match the table Db2 already has. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration.

Each entry in queries produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. Keep those three lists in the same order. Queries run when the publisher is triggered. They are not a continuous change feed. To read incrementally, put named parameters such as :last_id in the query, set their first values with initial_values, and save the next values with ctx.set_attr() after each successful run.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" keeps the rows already in the destination and inserts the returned rows. "replace" truncates the table before inserting. Neither mode changes an existing table's schema, so column additions, removals, and type changes need a database migration before the subscriber runs.

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set trigger_by to change when the function runs. Tabsdata checks the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not connect to Db2 then. A bad host, credential, query, or permission fails when the function runs. Every function in the collection uses the same connection. Use another collection when functions need another database or another set of credentials.

The Db2 CDC connector lets Tabsdata capture the changes made to Db2 tables (inserts, updates and deletes) and publish them into Tabsdata tables. With start_from="full", the stream starts with a full load: it takes a consistent snapshot of the tracked tables and then switches to change capture from the exact point of that snapshot, with no gaps and no duplicates. The full load and the change capture are one stream publisher, so there is nothing to reconcile between them. The Db2CdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to read the change-data (CD) tables that Db2 SQL Replication fills, and write every captured change into a Tabsdata table. Unlike Db2Src, which runs queries on a trigger, a CDC source runs continuously: registering the stream publisher starts a long-lived worker that keeps reading the CD tables until the function is disabled or deleted.

The Db2CdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to capture changes from Db2 into Tabsdata tables. See the full publisher walkthrough The stream publisher is registered in a collection created with a Db2CdcStreamSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

Db2 CDC builds on Db2 SQL Replication: the ASN Capture program (asncap) reads the Db2 log and copies each change of a registered table into that table's CD table. Tabsdata reads the CD tables. SQL Replication is set up in the source database: the ASN capture control tables exist, and asncap is running. Each tracked source table is registered for capture (a row in ASN.IBMSNAP_REGISTER), with an active registration and its own CD table. Every column is registered with its before-image; a registration without before-images is refused. The connecting user can SELECT the CD tables and ASN.IBMSNAP_REGISTER, ASN.IBMSNAP_PRUNCNTL and ASN.IBMSNAP_RESTART, and ASN.IBMSNAP_UOW when starting from "tail" or a timestamp. For start_from="full", the connecting user can also SELECT every tracked source table and EXECUTE the SYSPROC.MON_GET_TRANSACTION_LOG table function (for example through the SYSMON authority), and no tracked table is registered to capture updates as a delete plus an insert (CHG_UPD_TO_DEL_INS = 'Y').

Configure Db2CdcStreamSrc as the source of a @stream_publisher function to select the CD tables whose changes Tabsdata captures. stream_sales_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.db2 import Db2CdcStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @stream_publisher( source=Db2CdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "ASN.CD_ORDERS", "ASN.CD_CUSTOMERS", ], start_from="full", ), batch_max_secs=120, output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], ) def stream_sales_changes( orders: TableFramesSpec, customers: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return concat(orders), concat(customers) tables:list[str]required start_from:"full" | "head" | "tail" | CommitSeqPosition | TableCommitSeqPosition | TimestampPositionrequired columns_format:"columns" | "struct" | "map"optional flatten_columns:booloptional src_cfg:dictoptional batch_max_secs=120 hands the captured changes to the function at least every two minutes. The batch_* parameters decide when a batch of changes is handed to the function, and are the same for every stream source. See Stream Publishers for all of them. A stream publisher differs from a regular publisher in three ways: It has no trigger. Registering it starts the stream worker, which runs until the function is disabled or deleted. Each element of tables is one function parameter, and each parameter receives a list of frames: the changes captured for that table since the previous batch. Fold them with concat, which also returns None when the batch carried nothing for that table. The function must not declare a ctx parameter.

tables​ Defines the CD tables to read, as qualified cd_schema.cd_table names. These are the change-data tables, not the source tables. The connector finds each CD table's source table through ASN.IBMSNAP_REGISTER. Db2 folds unquoted names to uppercase, so write them in uppercase. Each element in tables represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function and to an entry in output_tables. For example: Db2CdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "ASN.CD_ORDERS", "ASN.CD_CUSTOMERS", ], start_from="tail", ) start_from​ Where the stream starts the first time it runs. Later runs resume from the position the stream has recorded, which it keeps for each CD table separately. "full": a full load of every tracked source table, then the changes captured after it. See Full load. "tail": only changes captured after the stream starts. "head": every change still in each CD table. CommitSeqPosition(seq="..."): one commit sequence for every table, as the hex form of the 16-byte IBMSNAP_COMMITSEQ value. TableCommitSeqPosition(seqs={"ASN.CD_ORDERS": "...", ...}): a commit sequence per CD table, for example after re-snapshotting some tables. Every CD table in tables must be listed; a table left out fails the stream. TimestampPosition(ts=...): from the first commit at or after a point in time, looked up in ASN.IBMSNAP_UOW. A naive datetime is read in the Db2 server's time zone. Full load​ With start_from="full", the stream first emits every row of each tracked source table and then captures the changes from the exact position of that snapshot. The snapshot is consistent across all the tracked tables, and no change is missed or repeated between the snapshot and the change capture. Each table's snapshot is preceded by one LOAD row (@td.cdc.meta.op = "l"), and its rows arrive as inserts. A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. The full load reads the source tables rather than the CD tables, and locks nothing. The changes committed while the tables are read are taken from the CD tables and reconciled with the rows read, so that every change is published once. asncap must be running, since the load waits for Capture to reach the end of the load before handing over to the change stream. To resynchronize a destination later, keep start_from="full" and reset the function's stage: tdk fn update --reset-stage <other options> The stream then starts again with a new full load and its LOAD rows. Resetting the stage with any other start_from restarts at that position and sends no LOAD row. columns_format​ How each change row lays out the table's column values: "columns" (the default), "struct" or "map". See Change rows. flatten_columns​ When True (the default), the new column values are written as ordinary top-level columns, so each change row reads like a row of the source table. columns_format then only shapes the old values. See Change rows. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. Only these keys are accepted: Key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10000 Rows buffered in the worker before they are written out to a file. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes none Bytes buffered before they are written out. Measuring bytes costs time on every change; prefer bounding by rows. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Longest time a change waits in the buffer. tabsdata.cdc.poll.max_secs 1 Longest time one read of the CD tables waits for changes. tabsdata.cdc.poll.idle_secs 1 Pause after a read that found no changes. tabsdata.cdc.fetch_size 100000 Rows fetched per round trip. tabsdata.cdc.chunk_size 100000 Rows per chunk while writing the full load. tabsdata.cdc.initial_load.max_window_changes 100000 Most changes that may be committed to the tracked tables while the full load reads them. Above it, the load fails; run it again at a quieter time or raise the limit. db2.cdc.logging_level 40 Logging verbosity of the connector, as a Python logging level number (10 debug, 20 info, 30 warning, 40 error). The buffer settings control when captured changes are written to files inside the worker. When those files are handed to the function is controlled by the batch parameters of @stream_publisher.

Every row the stream emits is one change. Besides the column values, each row carries change metadata: Column Type Description @td.cdc.meta.op str The operation: "i" insert, "u" update, "d" delete, "l" load (start of a full load). @td.cdc.meta.tx str The commit sequence of the transaction, in hex. Full load rows carry initial-load. @td.cdc.meta.sq int The change's sequence (IBMSNAP_INTENTSEQ). @td.cdc.meta.ts datetime (UTC) When the transaction committed. Full load rows carry the time the snapshot was taken. @td.cdc.meta.seg decimal The transaction's commit sequence (IBMSNAP_COMMITSEQ). Full load rows carry -1. @td.cdc.meta.ord decimal The change's sequence (IBMSNAP_INTENTSEQ). Ordering by seg and then ord gives the order the changes were committed in. @td.cdc.meta.fmt str The columns_format the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.flat bool The flatten_columns setting the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.sch str A hash of the source table's schema when the change was captured. It changes when the table's columns change. The column values are laid out according to flatten_columns and columns_format: New values Old values flatten_columns=True (default) One top-level column per source column, with the source column's name. Depends on columns_format. columns_format="columns" (default) @td.cdc.data.col.new.<column> per column, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.col.old.<column> per column. columns_format="struct" @td.cdc.data.row.new, one struct, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.row.old, one struct. columns_format="map" @td.cdc.data.map.new, a JSON object as a string, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.map.old, a JSON object as a string. What each operation carries: Operation New values Old values Insert (i) The inserted row. Empty. Update (u) The row after the update. The row before the update. Delete (d) The deleted row. Empty. Load (l) Empty. Empty. Empty values are null columns with "columns", a struct whose fields are all null with "struct", and a JSON object whose values are all null with "map". A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. SQL Replication does not copy LOB or XML values into the CD tables, so those columns always arrive as null. Use "columns" with flatten_columns=True for changes that land in a table and get queried. Use "struct" or "map" when the source table's schema may change while the stream runs, to carry the values opaquely instead of changing the output table's columns.

The stream reads only what asncap has captured. If Capture stops, the stream sees no new changes until it is running again. If a tracked table is deregistered, its registration is deactivated, Capture cold-starts, or pruning removes CD rows the stream has not read yet, the stream fails with an error explaining what happened. The fix is to restore the registration if needed and run a new full load: reset the stage with start_from="full". A CD table added to tables after the stream started has no recorded position, so the stream fails until a new full load runs.

The Druid Overlord API is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The Overlord credentials can submit and inspect ingestion tasks. Tabsdata can write to the S3 or Azure staging location and Druid can read the staged Parquet files.

Configure DruidDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which datasources Tabsdata writes in Druid. write_events.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.druid import DruidDest @subscriber( destination=DruidDest( tables=[ "events", ], ), input_tables=["events"], ) def write_events(events: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return events tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:"append" | "replace"optional time_column:stroptional segment_granularity:stroptional max_concurrent_subtasks:intoptional max_rows_per_segment:intoptional max_rows_in_memory:intoptional http_timeout_sec:intoptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Defines the Druid datasources the subscriber writes to. Each name is 1 to 128 characters, does not start with . or _, and contains no /, backslash or NUL. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. if_table_exists​ "append" (the default) adds rows to the datasource. "replace" overwrites it. time_column​ The column Druid uses as its primary __time field. Druid requires a time column on every datasource; when the rows have none, leave time_column unset and the ingest time is used instead. segment_granularity​ The time span of each Druid segment: ALL (the default), NONE, SECOND, MINUTE, FIFTEEN_MINUTE, THIRTY_MINUTE, HOUR, SIX_HOUR, DAY, WEEK, MONTH, QUARTER or YEAR. max_concurrent_subtasks, max_rows_per_segment, max_rows_in_memory and http_timeout_sec​ Tuning for the ingestion task: its concurrency (default 1), the row cap per segment (default 5000000), the in-memory row cap per task (default 1000000), and the HTTP request timeout in seconds (default 300). dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration. The accepted keys are druid.logging_level, druid.poll_interval_seconds, druid.retry_attempts and druid.retry_backoff_seconds.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" adds data to the datasource. "replace" overwrites it. time_column selects the row timestamp used as Druid __time; without it, the connector uses the ingest time.

The connection is to the Overlord API, not a SQL endpoint. A write finishes only after the submitted ingestion task finishes. http_timeout_sec, polling, retry, and backoff settings control how Tabsdata waits for it. segment_granularity and the row limits change the ingestion task, not the Tabsdata input table. Tabsdata does not contact Druid or the staging service when the collection is created. Those checks happen when the subscriber runs.

Druid subscribers use DruidDestConn to define the Overlord, the credentials, and the cloud storage the data is staged in. conn-druid.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.druid:DruidDestConn spec: overlord_url: 'http://druid-overlord.internal:8081' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_writer' password: 'secret:example-password' staging: kind: druidS3Location apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.druid:S3Location spec: bucket: 'acme-staging' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:example-access-key' secret_access_key: 'secret:example-secret-key' base_path: '/druid' overlord_url:strrequired credentials:UserPasswordrequired staging:CloudLocationrequired conn_cfg:dictoptional

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type druid-bulk-out --file conn-druid.yaml Edit the template file with the Druid connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-druid.yaml tdk collection create --name druid_out --conn-file conn-druid.yaml Then register the subscriber in the collection: tdk fn register --coll druid_out --path write_events.py::write_events The collection goes in the destinations group, because the connection is a destination connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be destinations. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Accepts secret: too. credentials​ A UserPassword used for HTTP basic authentication with the Overlord. The GCSSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from Google Cloud Storage into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a GCSSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Publisher connection, at the end of this page.

The bucket exists and is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The service account can list the bucket and read every object matched by paths. The object format and compression match format and format_cfg.

paths​ Defines the files that the publisher reads from Google Cloud Storage. Each path is relative to the base_path configured in GCSSrcConn. Source paths: cannot begin or end with / cannot contain empty path segments can contain a * glob in the final path segment For example: GCSSrc( paths=[ "orders/2026/*.parquet", "customers/customers.csv", ] ) Each element in paths represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function. When a path uses a glob to match multiple files, the matching files are provided through the corresponding publisher input. format​ Sets the format used to read the source files. Supported formats are AUTO, CSV, JSON, AVRO, PARQUET, and LOG. The default is AUTO, which determines the format from the file extension. format_cfg​ Sets format-specific reader options. Configuration is keyed by SrcFileFormat. initial_last_modified​ Sets the initial cutoff for incremental ingestion. On the first run, Tabsdata imports files modified at or after the specified timestamp. The cutoff then advances so subsequent runs only import newer files. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. The following options are supported: Option Description tabsdata.file.chunk_size Controls the size of chunks used when reading files. tabsdata.src_metadata.drop When True, excludes the @td.file.path metadata column. By default, rows read from Google Cloud Storage include a @td.file.path metadata column containing the source file's URI.

The GCSDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Google Cloud Storage. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a GCSDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Subscriber connection, at the end of this page.

The bucket exists and is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The service account can create and write objects under the configured base_path. The destination path is relative and does not contain a glob.

Configure GCSDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define where Tabsdata writes files in Google Cloud Storage. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.gcs import GCSDest, DestFileFormat @subscriber( destination=GCSDest( paths=[ "exports/orders.parquet", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders paths:list[str]required format:DestFileFormatoptional format_cfg:dictoptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

paths​ Defines where the subscriber writes files in Google Cloud Storage. Each path is relative to the base_path configured in GCSDestConn. Destination paths: cannot begin or end with / cannot contain empty path segments cannot contain globs Each element in paths represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Destination paths can contain variables that Tabsdata substitutes when the subscriber runs: Variable Value ${EXEC_PLAN_ID} Current execution plan ID. ${TRX_ID} Current transaction ID. ${EXEC_PLAN_TS} Timestamp when the execution plan started. For example: GCSDest( paths=[ "exports/${EXEC_PLAN_ID}/orders.parquet", ] ) Dynamic paths can be used to create a new object for each execution instead of overwriting an existing object. format​ Sets the format used to write the destination file. Supported formats are AUTO, CSV, JSON, AVRO, and PARQUET. The default is AUTO, which determines the format from the destination file extension. format_cfg​ Sets format-specific writer options. Configuration is keyed by DestFileFormat. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration. The tabsdata.file.chunk_size option controls the size of chunks used when writing files.

Each entry in a publisher's paths is one source slot. A literal path reads one object; a final-segment * glob can read several. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. initial_last_modified sets the cutoff for the first run. After a successful run, Tabsdata advances the cutoff so the same unchanged objects are not published again. Each entry in a subscriber's paths is one destination slot and maps by position to a returned value. Use ${EXEC_PLAN_ID}, ${TRX_ID}, or ${EXEC_PLAN_TS} in a path when every run needs a new object. A fixed path writes to the same location again.

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set trigger_by to change when the function runs. Tabsdata validates the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not contact Google Cloud Storage then. A bad path, credential, or permission fails when the function runs. Globs are allowed only for publisher source paths, and only in the final path segment. Subscriber destination paths cannot contain globs. All configured paths are relative to the connection's base_path.

The Kafka connector lets Tabsdata read messages from Kafka topics as they arrive, and publish them into Tabsdata tables. The KafkaStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to consume a topic, decode its messages from JSON, Avro or Protobuf, with or without a schema registry, and write them into a Tabsdata table. Unlike a regular publisher, which runs on a trigger, a Kafka source runs continuously: registering the stream publisher starts a long-lived worker that keeps consuming the topic until the function is disabled or deleted.

The KafkaStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to publish Kafka messages into Tabsdata tables. See the full publisher walkthrough The stream publisher is registered in a collection created with a KafkaStreamSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The brokers are reachable from the Tabsdata server. The connecting principal can Describe and Read the topic (every matching topic, for a regular expression), Read the consumer group, and read the cluster metadata. With a dlq_topic, the principal can also Describe and Write the dead letter topic, and the topic exists. The connector does not create it. With a Confluent schema registry, the registry user can read schemas. With an AWS Glue schema registry, the AWS credentials allow glue:GetSchemaVersion and glue:GetSchemaByDefinition, and also glue:RegisterSchemaVersion and glue:CreateSchema unless the schema given in the publisher is already registered. See schema.

Configure KafkaStreamSrc as the source of a @stream_publisher function to select the topic Tabsdata consumes. read_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.kafka import KafkaStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat ORDER_SCHEMA = """ { "type": "object", "properties": { "order_id": {"type": "integer"}, "customer": {"type": "string"}, "amount": {"type": "number"} }, "required": ["order_id", "customer", "amount"] } """ @stream_publisher( source=KafkaStreamSrc( topic="orders", data_format="json", schema=ORDER_SCHEMA, ), batch_max_secs=120, output_tables=["orders"], ) def read_orders(orders: TableFramesSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return concat(orders, how="diagonal_relaxed") topic:strrequired data_format:"json" | "avro" | Protobufrequired schema:strrequired dlq_topic:stroptional src_cfg:dictoptional batch_max_secs=120 hands the consumed messages to the function at least every two minutes. The batch_* parameters decide when a batch of messages is handed to the function, and are the same for every stream source. See Stream Publishers for all of them. A stream publisher differs from a regular publisher in three ways: It has no trigger. Registering it starts the stream worker, which runs until the function is disabled or deleted. A Kafka source has a single slot, so the function has a single parameter. It receives a list of frames: the messages consumed since the previous batch. Fold them with concat, which also returns None when the batch carried no messages. The function must not declare a ctx parameter. The table names come from output_tables, not from the topic.

topic​ The topic to consume. A name starting with ^ is a regular expression, and the stream consumes every topic that matches it, all into the same slot. The @td.kafka.topic column of each row tells which topic the message came from. data_format​ How the message values are encoded: "json": a JSON object per message. "avro": Avro. Protobuf(message_name="<package>.<Message>"): Protobuf. message_name is the full name of the message type, including the .proto package: com.example.Order, not Order. from tabsdatak.conn.kafka import KafkaStreamSrc, Protobuf KafkaStreamSrc( topic="orders", data_format=Protobuf(message_name="com.example.Order"), schema=ORDER_PROTO, ) schema​ The schema of the messages, as a string. What it is used for depends on the format and on the connection's schema registry: Format No schema registry Confluent AWS Glue "json" A JSON Schema. Every message is validated against it. An empty string skips validation. A JSON Schema the messages are validated against. An empty string validates against the registry's schema. Used to find the schema in the registry. Messages are validated against the registry's schema. "avro" The Avro schema the messages were written with. The schema to read the messages as (Avro reader schema). An empty string reads them as written. Used to find the schema in the registry. Messages are read with the registry's schema. Protobuf The .proto definition. The .proto definition. The .proto definition. A .proto definition is compiled on its own: it cannot import other files, including the Google well-known types such as google/protobuf/timestamp.proto. With AWS Glue, the stream looks the schema up in the registry each time it starts. If the registry does not have it, the stream registers it as a new version of schema_name, or creates schema_name if it does not exist. The schema is not checked when the function is defined. A malformed schema fails the stream when it starts. The schema does not set the column types of the output table. They come from the decoded values; see Message rows. dlq_topic​ A dead letter topic. A message that cannot be decoded, does not match the schema, or does not fit the column types of the batch is written to this topic, and the stream carries on. Without a dlq_topic, such a message stops the stream. Tabsdata restarts the stream after a while, but it stops again on the same message, so set a dlq_topic for any topic that may carry malformed messages. Each dead letter is a JSON object with the original value (original_value), the error (error), and the message's topic, partition, offset and timestamp. A message that was decoded but did not fit the column types carries the decoded message in record instead of original_value. The message key is kept for decoding errors. Headers are not copied. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. Only these keys are accepted: Key Default Description tabsdata.kafka.buffer.max_rows 10000 Messages buffered in the worker before they are written out to a file. tabsdata.kafka.buffer.max_bytes none Bytes buffered before they are written out, measured on the decoded messages. tabsdata.kafka.buffer.max_secs 60 Longest time a message waits in the buffer. tabsdata.kafka.poll.max_secs 2 Longest time one read of the topic takes. tabsdata.kafka.poll.idle_secs 0 Pause after a read that found no messages. tabsdata.kafka.consume.max_messages 10000 Most messages fetched from the brokers at once. kafka.connect_timeout_secs 16 Seconds to wait for the brokers when the stream starts, and for the dead letter topic to acknowledge writes. kafka.logging_level 40 Logging verbosity of the connector, as a Python logging level number (10 debug, 20 info, 30 warning, 40 error). The buffer settings control when consumed messages are written to files inside the worker. When those files are handed to the function is controlled by the batch parameters of @stream_publisher.

Each message becomes one row: the fields of the decoded message value, as columns sorted by name, plus one metadata column: Column Type Description @td.kafka.topic str The topic the message came from. The message key, headers, timestamp, partition and offset are not part of the row. Column types come from the decoded values: JSON: integers are int64, numbers are int64 or float64, strings are strings (a date in a string stays a string), objects are structs and arrays are lists. Avro: Avro types map to their Arrow counterparts, including logical types: timestamp-millis becomes a UTC timestamp and date a date. Protobuf: messages are converted the way Protobuf converts them to JSON: int64 and uint64 fields become strings, bytes become base64 strings, enums become their names, and fields left at their default value are included. A message with a null value, such as a compaction tombstone, cannot be decoded and goes to the dlq_topic. The function can receive several frames in one batch. A new frame starts when the messages change shape: without a schema registry, when a message has a field the frame does not; with a registry, when the schema version changes. Combine them with concat(frames, how="diagonal_relaxed"), which fills the missing columns with nulls. Within a frame, the first messages fix the column types. A later message whose values do not fit them goes to the dlq_topic.
There is no start position to configure. The stream resumes from the offsets committed to the consumer group; a group with none starts from the earliest message the topic retains.

A Kafka stream is at least once. The stream commits the offsets of a batch once the batch is handed over. If the stream stops between handing over a batch and committing it, the messages of that batch are published again after the restart, so remove duplicates downstream if they matter. Disabling the function stops the stream. Messages read but not yet handed over are read again when it is enabled.

Every stream publisher in a collection consumes with the group_id of the collection's connection, so Kafka treats them as members of one consumer group: Two stream publishers that read the same topic split its partitions between them, and each publishes only part of the messages. Stream publishers that read different topics each get all the partitions of their own topic, and their committed offsets do not mix. They still take part in each other's rebalances whenever one of them starts, stops or restarts. With the connector's default partition.assignment.strategy (cooperative-sticky), the others keep their partitions. With an eager strategy set in conn_cfg (range or roundrobin), every rebalance takes all partitions from every member, and each stream publisher hands over what it has read as an early batch (see Rebalances). The same applies to collections whose connections use the same group_id. Give each stream publisher that reads a topic its own collection, with its own group_id.

tdk fn update --reset-stage does not rewind a Kafka stream, because its position is the consumer group's. To read a topic again, update the collection's connection with a new group_id, which makes every stream publisher in the collection start over, or reset the group's offsets for that topic with the Kafka tools while the function is disabled.
When the brokers move partitions away from the stream, everything read from them so far is handed over at once, even before batch_min_secs has passed.

Messages the brokers delete before the stream reads them are skipped. If the brokers expire the group's offsets while the stream is stopped, the stream starts again from the earliest message retained.

If the brokers cannot be reached when the stream starts, or a schema registry cannot be reached while decoding, the stream stops without committing, and Tabsdata restarts it after a while. Nothing is sent to the dlq_topic for these errors. The stream warns in its log when the time between two reads of the topic gets close to the consumer's max.poll.interval.ms. Raise it in conn_cfg if batches take long to hand over.

Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: KafkaStreamSrc for a collection created with KafkaStreamSrcConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name orders_kafka --conn-file conn-kafka.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project. Every stream publisher in the collection consumes with the connection's group_id. Two stream publishers of one collection that read the same topic would split its partitions between them, each publishing only part of the messages. Give each stream publisher that reads a topic its own collection, with its own group_id. See One consumer group per collection.

servers​ The bootstrap servers, as a comma-separated list of host:port. Written as a plain value here, but accepts secret: too. group_id​ The Kafka consumer group the stream consumes with. The stream commits its progress to this group, and resumes from it after a restart. A group_id with no committed offsets starts from the earliest message the topic retains. Written as a plain value here, but accepts secret: too. The consumer group belongs to the connection, not to the function: every stream publisher registered in the collection consumes with this same group_id. See One consumer group per collection. credentials​ A user and password for SASL authentication. With credentials, the connector uses SCRAM-SHA-256 over SASL_PLAINTEXT, which does not encrypt the connection, and ignores any security.protocol or sasl.mechanism in conn_cfg. For TLS, another SASL mechanism, or mutual TLS, leave credentials out and set the client properties in conn_cfg instead. schema_registry​ The schema registry the messages are encoded against. Leave it out for messages encoded without a registry. It is a mapping with the fields of one of two registry kinds, recognized by their fields. A Confluent schema registry takes a required url, optional credentials (UserPassword), and optional configs with extra Confluent schema registry client properties: schema_registry: url: 'https://registry.internal:8081' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:registry_user' password: 'secret:example-password' An AWS Glue schema registry takes a required region_name, credentials (AwsAccessSecretKey), registry_name and schema_name, and optional configs with extra keyword arguments for the AWS Glue client, such as endpoint_url: schema_registry: region_name: 'us-east-1' registry_name: 'orders-registry' schema_name: 'orders' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:AKIAEXAMPLE' secret_access_key: 'secret:example-secret-key' conn_cfg​ Kafka client properties, as librdkafka names them, for example security.protocol, ssl.ca.location, sasl.mechanism or sasl.username. The Local File System connector lets Tabsdata read files from and write files to the server's own filesystem. The LocalFileSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from local files into a Tabsdata table. The LocalFileDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into local files.
Format Publish Subscribe AUTO? Yes Yes CSV Yes Yes JSON Yes Yes AVRO Yes Yes PARQUET Yes Yes LOG Yes No

The LocalFileSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from local files into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a LocalFileSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Publisher connection, at the end of this page.

The configured base_path exists on the Tabsdata server and is readable by the function worker. Every source path stays under base_path; parent-directory segments are refused. The file format and compression match format and format_cfg.

Configure LocalFileSrc as the source of a publisher function to select the files that Tabsdata reads from disk. publish_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher from tabsdatak.conn.localfile import LocalFileSrc, SrcFileFormat @publisher( source=LocalFileSrc( paths=[ "incoming/orders.parquet", ], ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders): return orders paths:list[str]required format:SrcFileFormatoptional format_cfg:dictoptional initial_last_modified:datetimeoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

paths​ Defines the files that the publisher reads from disk. Each path is relative to the base_path configured in LocalFileSrcConn. Source paths: cannot begin or end with / cannot contain empty path segments can contain a * glob in the final path segment For example: LocalFileSrc( paths=[ "orders/2026/*.parquet", "customers/customers.csv", ] ) Each element in paths represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function. When a path uses a glob to match multiple files, the matching files are provided through the corresponding publisher input. format​ Sets the format used to read the source files. Supported formats are AUTO, CSV, JSON, AVRO, PARQUET, and LOG. The default is AUTO, which determines the format from the file extension. format_cfg​ Sets format-specific reader options. Configuration is keyed by SrcFileFormat. initial_last_modified​ Sets the initial cutoff for incremental ingestion. On the first run, Tabsdata imports files modified at or after the specified timestamp. The cutoff then advances so subsequent runs only import newer files. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. The following options are supported: Option Description tabsdata.file.chunk_size Controls the size of chunks used when reading files. tabsdata.src_metadata.drop When True, excludes the @td.file.path metadata column. By default, rows read from disk include a @td.file.path metadata column containing the source file's path.

The LocalFileDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into local files. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a LocalFileDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Subscriber connection, at the end of this page.

The configured base_path exists on the Tabsdata server and is writable by the function worker. Every destination path stays under base_path; parent-directory segments and globs are refused. Enough disk space is available for the files written by the run.

Configure LocalFileDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define where Tabsdata writes files on disk. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.localfile import LocalFileDest, DestFileFormat @subscriber( destination=LocalFileDest( paths=[ "exports/orders.parquet", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders paths:list[str]required format:DestFileFormatoptional format_cfg:dictoptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

paths​ Defines where the subscriber writes files on disk. Each path is relative to the base_path configured in LocalFileDestConn. Destination paths: cannot begin or end with / cannot contain empty path segments cannot contain globs Each element in paths represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Destination paths can contain variables that Tabsdata substitutes when the subscriber runs: Variable Value ${EXEC_PLAN_ID} Current execution plan ID. ${TRX_ID} Current transaction ID. ${EXEC_PLAN_TS} Timestamp when the execution plan started. For example: LocalFileDest( paths=[ "exports/${EXEC_PLAN_ID}/orders.parquet", ] ) Dynamic paths can be used to create a new file for each execution instead of overwriting an existing one. format​ Sets the format used to write the destination file. Supported formats are AUTO, CSV, JSON, AVRO, and PARQUET. The default is AUTO, which determines the format from the destination file extension. format_cfg​ Sets format-specific writer options. Configuration is keyed by DestFileFormat. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration. The tabsdata.file.chunk_size option controls the size of chunks used when writing files.

Each entry in a publisher's paths is one source slot. A literal path reads one file; a final-segment * glob can read several. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. initial_last_modified sets the cutoff for the first run. After a successful run, Tabsdata advances the cutoff so the same unchanged files are not published again. Each entry in a subscriber's paths is one destination slot and maps by position to a returned value. Use ${EXEC_PLAN_ID}, ${TRX_ID}, or ${EXEC_PLAN_TS} in a path when every run needs a new file. A fixed path writes to the same location again.

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set trigger_by to change when the function runs. Tabsdata validates the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not contact local filesystem then. A bad path, credential, or permission fails when the function runs. Globs are allowed only for publisher source paths, and only in the final path segment. Subscriber destination paths cannot contain globs. All configured paths are relative to the connection's base_path.

Local File System publishers use LocalFileSrcConn to define the root filesystem path used by the publisher. Unlike the cloud storage connectors, there is no bucket and no credentials: the connector reads directly off the server's own disk. conn-local-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.localfile:LocalFileSrcConn spec: base_path: '/data/hr' base_path:strrequired conn_cfg:dictoptional

Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: LocalFileSrc for a collection created with LocalFileSrcConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name local_in --conn-file conn-local-in.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

The MySQLDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into MariaDB. warning The MariaDB connector needs the mysql-connector-python driver, which Tabsdata does not redistribute. The MySQLSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read data from MariaDB into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a MySQLSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Publisher connection, at the end of this page.
The MariaDB server is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The connection user can run every query in queries and read every referenced table or view.

Configure MySQLSrc as the source of a publisher function to select the queries that Tabsdata runs against MariaDB. publish_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc @publisher( source=MySQLSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM orders", ], ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders): return orders queries:list[str]required initial_values:dictoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

queries​ Defines the SQL queries the publisher runs against MariaDB. Each element in queries represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function. For example: MySQLSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM country", "SELECT * FROM city", ], ) initial_values​ The first-run values for named parameters in queries, written :name. On later runs each parameter takes the value the publisher stored with ctx.set_attr(name, value), so a query can read only the rows added since the last run. Parameters bind values such as IDs and timestamps, not identifiers. Schema and table names have to be written into the query. For example: from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TrxCtx, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLSrc @publisher( source=MySQLSrc( queries=["SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id > :last_id ORDER BY id"], initial_values={"last_id": 0}, ), output_tables=["orders"], ) def publish_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec, ctx: TrxCtx) -> TableFrameSpec: row = orders.max_for("id") if row is not None and row["id"] is not None: ctx.set_attr("last_id", int(row["id"])) return orders src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration.

The MySQLDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into MariaDB. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a MySQLDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Subscriber connection, at the end of this page.

The MariaDB server is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The connection user can create missing destination tables and insert rows. With if_table_exists="replace", it can also truncate existing tables.

Configure MySQLDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in MariaDB. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLDest @subscriber( destination=MySQLDest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:stroptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in MariaDB. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. For example: MySQLDest( tables=[ "vendors", "items", ], ) if_table_exists​ Controls what happens when the destination table already has rows. "append" (the default) keeps inserting into the existing rows. "replace" truncates the table before inserting. Neither mode changes the destination table's schema, so the returned frame's columns need to match the table MariaDB already has. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration.

Each entry in queries produces one source slot. The slots map by position to the publisher function arguments and then to output_tables. Keep those three lists in the same order. Queries run when the publisher is triggered. They are not a continuous change feed. To read incrementally, put named parameters such as :last_id in the query, set their first values with initial_values, and save the next values with ctx.set_attr() after each successful run.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" keeps the rows already in the destination and inserts the returned rows. "replace" truncates the table before inserting. Neither mode changes an existing table's schema, so column additions, removals, and type changes need a database migration before the subscriber runs.

Without trigger_by, a publisher runs only when triggered manually, while a subscriber runs when any input table commits. Set trigger_by to change when the function runs. Tabsdata checks the connection document when the collection is created, but it does not connect to MariaDB then. A bad host, credential, query, or permission fails when the function runs. Every function in the collection uses the same connection. Use another collection when functions need another database or another set of credentials.

The MongoDB connector lets Tabsdata subscribers write data from Tabsdata tables into MongoDB collections, one document per row. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a MongoDBDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The MongoDB deployment is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The MongoDB user can create and write the target collections, and can drop them when replace mode is used. use_trxs=True requires a replica set or sharded cluster that supports transactions.

Configure MongoDBDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which MongoDB collections Tabsdata writes. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.mongodb import MongoDBDest @subscriber( destination=MongoDBDest( collections_with_ids=[("sales_db.orders", "order_id")], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return orders collections_with_ids:list[tuple[str, str | None]]required if_collection_exists:"append" | "replace"optional update_existing:booloptional use_trxs:booloptional docs_per_trx:intoptional maintain_order:booloptional fail_on_duplicate_key:booloptional log_intermediate_files:booloptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

collections_with_ids​ A list of (collection, id_field) pairs. collection is the target collection, written <database>.<collection> or as a bare <collection> in the database named in the connection URI. id_field is the field used as each document's _id; None lets MongoDB generate the ids. Each pair in collections_with_ids represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. if_collection_exists​ "append" (the default) leaves the existing documents in place. "replace" drops the collection before writing. update_existing​ When True (the default), a document whose id already exists is updated (an upsert). When False, documents are inserted and an existing id fails the batch. Ignored when id_field is None, since generated ids never collide. use_trxs and docs_per_trx​ docs_per_trx sets the documents per write batch, 1000 by default. With use_trxs=True, each batch is written in a MongoDB transaction, which requires a replica set. maintain_order​ When True, documents are inserted in input order. Slower, but the server-side order is deterministic. fail_on_duplicate_key​ When True (the default), a duplicate-key error fails the write. When False, it is logged and the batch continues. log_intermediate_files​ When True, each intermediate JSONL file is logged before upload, for debugging large writes. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration. The only accepted key is mongodb.logging_level. pymongo.* options go in the connection's conn_cfg.

Each (collection, id_field) entry in collections_with_ids is one destination slot. A named id_field becomes the document _id; None lets MongoDB generate it. if_collection_exists="append" keeps existing documents. "replace" drops the collection first. With update_existing=True, matching ids are upserted; with it disabled, the connector inserts and an id collision fails the batch.

docs_per_trx is both the write-batch size and, when transactions are enabled, the number of documents per transaction. maintain_order=True keeps input order but gives up some write throughput. fail_on_duplicate_key=False logs duplicate-key errors and continues the batch. Use it only when skipping those documents is acceptable. Tabsdata does not connect to MongoDB when the collection is created. URI, credential, topology, and permission errors appear when the subscriber runs.

Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name mongodb_out --conn-file conn-mongodb.yaml.
