The MySQL CDC connector lets Tabsdata capture the changes made to MySQL tables (inserts, updates, deletes and truncates) as they are committed, and publish them into Tabsdata tables. With start_from="full", the stream starts with a full load: it takes a consistent snapshot of the tracked tables and then switches to change capture from the exact point of that snapshot, with no gaps and no duplicates. The full load and the change capture are one stream publisher, so there is nothing to reconcile between them. The MySQLCdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to follow the MySQL binary log (binlog) as a replica would and write every captured change into a Tabsdata table. Unlike MySQLSrc, which runs queries on a trigger, a CDC source runs continuously: registering the stream publisher starts a long-lived worker that keeps reading the binlog until the function is disabled or deleted.

The MySQLCdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to capture changes from MySQL into Tabsdata tables. See the full publisher walkthrough The stream publisher is registered in a collection created with a MySQLCdcStreamSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The server's binlog is set up for row-based capture: log_bin = ON, binlog_format = ROW, binlog_row_image = FULL and gtid_mode = ON. The stream checks these at start and refuses a server that does not have them. The connecting user holds the replication privileges a binlog reader needs (REPLICATION SLAVE and REPLICATION CLIENT). When streaming from a replica, the replica runs with log_replica_updates = ON, and with replica_preserve_commit_order = ON if it applies transactions in parallel. For start_from="full", the connecting user also holds SELECT on every tracked table, and RELOAD where the server grants it, for the global read lock. The tracked tables are InnoDB. Managed services such as Amazon RDS and Aurora refuse the global read lock, and the full load still runs there with the same transactional consistency.

Configure MySQLCdcStreamSrc as the source of a @stream_publisher function to select the tables whose changes Tabsdata captures. stream_sales_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.mysql import MySQLCdcStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @stream_publisher( source=MySQLCdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "sales.orders", "sales.customers", ], start_from="full", ), batch_max_secs=120, output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], ) def stream_sales_changes( orders: TableFramesSpec, customers: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return concat(orders), concat(customers) tables:list[str]required start_from:"full" | "head" | "tail" | GtidPosition | BinlogPosition | TimestampPositionrequired columns_format:"columns" | "struct" | "map"optional flatten_columns:booloptional src_cfg:dictoptional batch_max_secs=120 hands the captured changes to the function at least every two minutes. The batch_* parameters decide when a batch of changes is handed to the function, and are the same for every stream source. See Stream Publishers for all of them. A stream publisher differs from a regular publisher in three ways: It has no trigger. Registering it starts the stream worker, which runs until the function is disabled or deleted. Each element of tables is one function parameter, and each parameter receives a list of frames: the changes captured for that table since the previous batch. Fold them with concat, which also returns None when the batch carried nothing for that table. The function must not declare a ctx parameter.

tables​ Defines the MySQL tables whose changes are captured, as qualified database.table names. Each element in tables represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function and to an entry in output_tables. For example: MySQLCdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "sales.orders", "sales.customers", ], start_from="tail", ) start_from​ Where the stream starts the first time it runs. Later runs resume from the position the stream has recorded. "full": a full load of every tracked table, then the changes committed after it. See Full load. "tail": only changes committed after the stream starts. "head": replay from the oldest change still in binlog retention. GtidPosition(gtid="<uuid>:<n>"): after a global transaction id. The given GTIDs count as already read, and the stream starts with the next transaction. A range such as "<uuid>:1-<n>" is accepted too. BinlogPosition(file="mysql-bin.000001", pos=4): from a binlog file and byte offset, as SHOW BINARY LOG STATUS or SHOW BINLOG EVENTS report them. Position 4 is the start of a file. TimestampPosition(ts=...): from the first binlog event at or after a point in time. A naive datetime is read as UTC. A time before the oldest retained binlog is refused. Full load​ With start_from="full", the stream first emits every row of each tracked table and then captures the changes from the exact binlog position of that snapshot. The snapshot is consistent across all the tracked tables, and no change is missed or repeated between the snapshot and the change capture. Each table's snapshot is preceded by one LOAD row (@td.cdc.meta.op = "l"), and its rows arrive as inserts. A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. The tables are read in one consistent-snapshot transaction. To pin that snapshot to a binlog position, the stream briefly takes the global read lock. The lock is held only while the position is read, not while the tables are scanned. On servers that refuse the lock, such as Amazon RDS and Aurora, the snapshot is just as consistent. To resynchronize a destination later, keep start_from="full" and reset the function's stage: tdk fn update --reset-stage <other options> The stream then starts again with a new full load and its LOAD rows. Resetting the stage with any other start_from restarts at that position and sends no LOAD row. columns_format​ How each change row lays out the table's column values: "columns" (the default), "struct" or "map". See Change rows. flatten_columns​ When True (the default), the new column values are written as ordinary top-level columns, so each change row reads like a row of the source table. columns_format then only shapes the old values. See Change rows. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. Only these keys are accepted: Key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10000 Rows buffered in the worker before they are written out to a file. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes none Bytes buffered before they are written out. Measuring bytes costs time on every change; prefer bounding by rows. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Longest time a change waits in the buffer. tabsdata.cdc.poll.max_secs 1 Longest time one read of the binlog waits for changes. tabsdata.cdc.poll.idle_secs 1 Pause after a read that found no changes. tabsdata.cdc.max_large_text_length 1024 Longest value, in characters, accepted from an unbounded text column. A longer value fails the stream. tabsdata.cdc.fetch_size 100000 Rows fetched per round trip while reading the full load. tabsdata.cdc.chunk_size 100000 Rows per chunk while writing the full load. mysql.cdc.logging_level 40 Logging verbosity of the connector, as a Python logging level number (10 debug, 20 info, 30 warning, 40 error). The buffer settings control when captured changes are written to files inside the worker. When those files are handed to the function is controlled by the batch parameters of @stream_publisher.

Every row the stream emits is one change. Besides the column values, each row carries change metadata: Column Type Description @td.cdc.meta.op str The operation: "i" insert, "u" update, "d" delete, "t" truncate, "l" load (start of a full load). @td.cdc.meta.tx str The transaction's GTID. Full load rows carry initial-load. @td.cdc.meta.sq int The change's sequence within its transaction. @td.cdc.meta.ts datetime (UTC) When the transaction committed. Full load rows carry the time the snapshot was taken. @td.cdc.meta.seg decimal The transaction's number in its GTID. Full load rows carry -1. @td.cdc.meta.ord decimal The position of the change within the transaction. Ordering by seg and then ord gives the order the changes were committed in. @td.cdc.meta.fmt str The columns_format the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.flat bool The flatten_columns setting the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.sch str A hash of the source table's schema when the change was captured. It changes when the table's columns change. The column values are laid out according to flatten_columns and columns_format: New values Old values flatten_columns=True (default) One top-level column per source column, with the source column's name. Depends on columns_format. columns_format="columns" (default) @td.cdc.data.col.new.<column> per column, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.col.old.<column> per column. columns_format="struct" @td.cdc.data.row.new, one struct, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.row.old, one struct. columns_format="map" @td.cdc.data.map.new, a JSON object as a string, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.map.old, a JSON object as a string. What each operation carries: Operation New values Old values Insert (i) The inserted row. Empty. Update (u) The row after the update. The complete row before the update. Delete (d) The deleted row. Empty. Truncate (t), Load (l) Empty. Empty. Empty values are null columns with "columns", a struct whose fields are all null with "struct", and a JSON object whose values are all null with "map". A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. A TRUNCATE row reports that the source table was truncated. BLOB columns are not captured: they always arrive as null. Use "columns" with flatten_columns=True for changes that land in a table and get queried. Use "struct" or "map" when the source table's schema may change while the stream runs, to carry the values opaquely instead of changing the output table's columns.

The Postgres CDC connector lets Tabsdata capture the changes made to Postgres tables (inserts, updates, deletes and truncates) as they are committed, and publish them into Tabsdata tables. With start_from="full", the stream starts with a full load: it takes a consistent snapshot of the tracked tables and then switches to change capture from the exact point of that snapshot, with no gaps and no duplicates. The full load and the change capture are one stream publisher, so there is nothing to reconcile between them. The PostgresCdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to follow the Postgres write-ahead log (WAL) through a logical replication slot and write every captured change into a Tabsdata table. Unlike PostgresSrc, which runs queries on a trigger, a CDC source runs continuously: registering the stream publisher starts a long-lived worker that keeps reading the WAL until the function is disabled or deleted.

The PostgresCdcStreamSrc connector can be used by a stream publisher function to capture changes from Postgres into Tabsdata tables. See the full publisher walkthrough The stream publisher is registered in a collection created with a PostgresCdcStreamSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The server runs with wal_level = logical. The wal2json logical decoding output plugin, version 2.0 or later, is installed on the server. The connecting role has the REPLICATION attribute. Every tracked table has a replica identity: a primary key that is not DEFERRABLE, or REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, or REPLICA IDENTITY USING INDEX on a unique index. A table without one is refused, because Postgres would drop its updates and deletes from the WAL. A tracked table with large text columns needs REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, or the postgres.cdc.unchanged_large_text_as_null setting described under src_cfg. For start_from="full", the connecting role can also SELECT every tracked table.

Configure PostgresCdcStreamSrc as the source of a @stream_publisher function to select the tables whose changes Tabsdata captures. stream_sales_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @stream_publisher( source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "public.orders", "public.customers", ], replication_slot="tabsdata_sales", start_from="full", ), batch_max_secs=120, output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], ) def stream_sales_changes( orders: TableFramesSpec, customers: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return concat(orders), concat(customers) tables:list[str]required replication_slot:strrequired start_from:"full" | "head" | "tail" | LsnPositionrequired replication_slot_behavior:"reuse" | "create"optional publication_name:stroptional columns_format:"columns" | "struct" | "map"optional flatten_columns:booloptional src_cfg:dictoptional batch_max_secs=120 hands the captured changes to the function at least every two minutes. The batch_* parameters decide when a batch of changes is handed to the function, and are the same for every stream source. See Stream Publishers for all of them. A stream publisher differs from a regular publisher in three ways: It has no trigger. Registering it starts the stream worker, which runs until the function is disabled or deleted. Each element of tables is one function parameter, and each parameter receives a list of frames: the changes captured for that table since the previous batch. Fold them with concat, which also returns None when the batch carried nothing for that table. The function must not declare a ctx parameter.

tables​ Defines the Postgres tables whose changes are captured, as qualified schema.table names. Each element in tables represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function and to an entry in output_tables. For example: PostgresCdcStreamSrc( tables=[ "public.orders", "public.customers", ], replication_slot="tabsdata_sales", start_from="tail", ) replication_slot​ The logical replication slot the stream reads through. Postgres keeps the WAL the slot has not yet consumed, which is what lets the stream resume where it left off after a restart. Each stream publisher needs its own slot. Tabsdata never drops the slot, not even when the function is deleted. A slot that is no longer read makes the server keep WAL indefinitely, so drop it with pg_drop_replication_slot('<slot>') once its stream is gone. start_from​ Where the stream starts the first time it runs. Later runs resume from the position the stream has recorded. "full": a full load of every tracked table, then the changes committed after it. See Full load. "tail": only changes committed after the stream starts. "head": replay from the oldest WAL the slot retains. LsnPosition(lsn=...): an explicit WAL position, given as the 64-bit integer that pg_current_wal_lsn() - '0/0'::pg_lsn returns. Full load​ With start_from="full", the stream first emits every row of each tracked table and then captures the changes from the exact position of that snapshot. The snapshot is consistent across all the tracked tables, and no change is missed or repeated between the snapshot and the change capture. Each table's snapshot is preceded by one LOAD row (@td.cdc.meta.op = "l"), and its rows arrive as inserts. A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. No table is locked. The snapshot is the one Postgres exports when a replication slot is created: the stream's own slot when the stream creates it, or otherwise a temporary slot that is created for the load and dropped once the load is read. To resynchronize a destination later, keep start_from="full" and reset the function's stage: tdk fn update --reset-stage <other options> The stream then starts again with a new full load and its LOAD rows. Resetting the stage with any other start_from restarts at that position and sends no LOAD row. replication_slot_behavior​ "reuse" (the default) requires the slot to exist already, for example when a DBA provisions it. "create" creates the slot, and does nothing if it already exists. publication_name​ A Postgres publication that scopes what the slot decodes (wal2json's publication_names option). columns_format​ How each change row lays out the table's column values: "columns" (the default), "struct" or "map". See Change rows. flatten_columns​ When True (the default), the new column values are written as ordinary top-level columns, so each change row reads like a row of the source table. columns_format then only shapes the old values. See Change rows. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. Only these keys are accepted: Key Default Description tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows 10000 Rows buffered in the worker before they are written out to a file. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_bytes none Bytes buffered before they are written out. Measuring bytes costs time on every change; prefer bounding by rows. tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_secs 60 Longest time a change waits in the buffer. tabsdata.cdc.poll.max_secs 1 Longest time one read of the WAL waits for changes. tabsdata.cdc.poll.idle_secs 1 Pause after a read that found no changes. tabsdata.cdc.max_large_text_length 1024 Longest value, in characters, accepted from an unbounded text column. A longer value fails the stream. tabsdata.cdc.fetch_size 100000 Rows fetched per round trip while reading the full load. tabsdata.cdc.chunk_size 100000 Rows per chunk while writing the full load. postgres.cdc.wal2json_format_version 2 wal2json output format, 1 or 2. Truncates are only captured with 2. postgres.cdc.unchanged_large_text_as_null unset Set to true to accept that, on a table without REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, an update that does not touch a large text column delivers that column as null. When unset, such a table refuses to start the stream. postgres.cdc.accept_gap unset Lets a stopped stream resume past one reported gap between its position and the slot's. Give the value exactly as the error message prints it; it matches no other gap. postgres.cdc.logging_level 40 Logging verbosity of the connector, as a Python logging level number (10 debug, 20 info, 30 warning, 40 error). The buffer settings control when captured changes are written to files inside the worker. When those files are handed to the function is controlled by the batch parameters of @stream_publisher.

Every row the stream emits is one change. Besides the column values, each row carries change metadata: Column Type Description @td.cdc.meta.op str The operation: "i" insert, "u" update, "d" delete, "t" truncate, "l" load (start of a full load). @td.cdc.meta.tx str The source transaction id. Full load rows carry initial-load. @td.cdc.meta.sq int The change's sequence within its transaction. @td.cdc.meta.ts datetime (UTC) When the transaction committed. Full load rows carry the time the snapshot was taken. @td.cdc.meta.seg decimal The position of the transaction's commit in the WAL. Full load rows carry -1. @td.cdc.meta.ord decimal The position of the change within the transaction. Ordering by seg and then ord gives the order the changes were committed in. @td.cdc.meta.fmt str The columns_format the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.flat bool The flatten_columns setting the row was produced with. @td.cdc.meta.sch str A hash of the source table's schema when the change was captured. It changes when the table's columns change. The column values are laid out according to flatten_columns and columns_format: New values Old values flatten_columns=True (default) One top-level column per source column, with the source column's name. Depends on columns_format. columns_format="columns" (default) @td.cdc.data.col.new.<column> per column, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.col.old.<column> per column. columns_format="struct" @td.cdc.data.row.new, one struct, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.row.old, one struct. columns_format="map" @td.cdc.data.map.new, a JSON object as a string, when not flattened. @td.cdc.data.map.old, a JSON object as a string. What each operation carries: Operation New values Old values Insert (i) The inserted row. Empty. Update (u) The row after the update. The row before the update. Postgres logs the complete previous row only for tables with REPLICA IDENTITY FULL; otherwise only the replica identity columns are present. Delete (d) The deleted row. Without REPLICA IDENTITY FULL, only the replica identity columns are present. Empty. Truncate (t), Load (l) Empty. Empty. Empty values are null columns with "columns", a struct whose fields are all null with "struct", and a JSON object whose values are all null with "map". A LOAD row tells the consumer to empty its copy of the table before applying the rows that follow. A TRUNCATE row reports that the source table was truncated. bytea and oid columns are not captured: they always arrive as null. Use "columns" with flatten_columns=True for changes that land in a table and get queried. Use "struct" or "map" when the source table's schema may change while the stream runs, to carry the values opaquely instead of changing the output table's columns.

Stopping a stream does not lose changes: the slot keeps the WAL, and the stream resumes from its recorded position. The server also keeps that WAL until the stream consumes it, or until the slot is dropped. If the slot is dropped or invalidated, the server is restored from a backup, or the stream's position no longer matches the server, the stream fails with an error explaining what happened. In most of those cases the fix is a new full load: reset the stage with start_from="full". A slot can only be read by one connection at a time. A stream whose slot is still held by another connection fails after a timeout.

Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: PostgresCdcStreamSrc for a collection created with PostgresCdcStreamSrcConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name sales_cdc --conn-file conn-postgres-cdc.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project. A batch PostgresSrc publisher cannot share this collection, because it uses a different connection (postgres-sql-in).

uri​ The SQLAlchemy-style connection URI: postgres://host:port/database (or postgresql://). Written as a plain value here, but accepts secret: too. credentials​ The database user and password, spliced into the URI at connect time. UserPassword requires a user and password. The role must have the REPLICATION attribute. entity_whitelist​ A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet: it does not limit which tables a stream can track. Leave it out. conn_cfg​ psycopg2 connection keywords such as sslmode, sslrootcert, connect_timeout or application_name. They apply to every connection the stream opens: catalog reads, the full load and the replication connection. The replication slot is configured on the publisher, not on the connection, so one connection can serve several stream publishers as long as each uses its own slot.

The Salesforce connectors let Tabsdata read data from Salesforce into Tabsdata tables. The SalesforceSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to run a SOQL query against Salesforce and write the result into a Tabsdata table. The SalesforceReportSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read Salesforce reports into Tabsdata tables. Both connectors use the same connection class, SalesforceSrcConn, so one collection can hold both kinds of publisher.

The SalesforceSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read the result of a SOQL query into a Tabsdata table. See the full publisher walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a SalesforceSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.
API access is enabled for the Salesforce user. The username, password, and security token are valid for the instance. The user can read every object and field referenced by the SOQL query.

Configure SalesforceSrc as the source of a publisher function to select the SOQL query that Tabsdata runs against Salesforce. publish_accounts.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceSrc @publisher( source=SalesforceSrc( queries=["SELECT Id, Name FROM Account"], ), output_tables=["accounts"], ) def publish_accounts(accounts: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return accounts queries:list[str]required include_deleted:booloptional initial_last_modified:datetimeoptional api_version:stroptional src_cfg:dictoptional

queries​ A list holding one SOQL query. The list currently takes exactly one entry, and its result maps to the one argument of the publisher function and the one entry in output_tables. include_deleted​ When True, the query also reads deleted rows, through the queryAll endpoint. Defaults to False. initial_last_modified​ A cutoff substituted for any $lastModified token in the query, for example WHERE SystemModStamp > $lastModified, so a run reads only the records changed after it. api_version​ Overrides the Salesforce API version, written <major>.<minor>, for example "60.0". src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. The accepted keys are salesforce.logging_level and tabsdata.src_metadata.drop.

The SalesforceReportSrc connector can be used by a publisher function to read Salesforce reports into Tabsdata tables. See the full report walkthrough The publisher is registered in a collection created with a SalesforceSrcConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

API access is enabled for the Salesforce user. The user can open every report in reports and read the fields used by its filters. Incremental reads need the last-modified column to be present in the report.

Configure SalesforceReportSrc as the source of a publisher function to select the reports that Tabsdata reads. publish_customers.py from tabsdatak.api import publisher, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceReportSrc @publisher( source=SalesforceReportSrc( reports=[ "00O000000000001", ], ), output_tables=["customers"], ) def publish_customers(customers: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return customers reports:list[str]required column_name_strategy:"columnName" | "label"optional find_report_by:"id" | "name"optional filter:list[tuple]optional filter_logic:stroptional last_modified_column:stroptional initial_last_modified:datetimeoptional src_cfg:dictoptional

reports​ The reports to read, as report ids (15 or 18 alphanumeric characters) or report names, as a non-empty list. Each element in reports represents one source slot and maps positionally to an argument in the publisher function and to an entry in output_tables. column_name_strategy​ "columnName" (the default) names the columns after the report's API column names. "label" uses the display labels. find_report_by​ How an entry of reports is looked up. Unset, an entry that looks like an id is looked up as an id and anything else as a name. "id" or "name" forces one lookup, for an entry that could be either. filter​ A list of (column, operator, value) triples applied on the Salesforce server before the report is downloaded. operator is one of equals, notEqual, lessThan, greaterThan, lessOrEqual, greaterOrEqual, contains, notContain, startsWith, includes or excludes. filter_logic​ A boolean expression over the filter entries, numbered from 1, for example "(1 AND 2) OR 3". last_modified_column and initial_last_modified​ An incremental read: only the rows whose last_modified_column is after initial_last_modified are read. Each of the two requires the other. src_cfg​ Sets additional source configuration. The accepted keys are salesforce.logging_level and tabsdata.src_metadata.drop.

SalesforceSrc.queries currently takes one SOQL query, which produces the publisher's one source slot. The selected Salesforce fields become columns in that slot. For incremental SOQL reads, include SystemModStamp in the selected fields and compare it with $lastModified. The first run uses initial_last_modified; later runs use the highest SystemModStamp already seen. Set include_deleted=True when deleted records also need to be returned. Each entry in SalesforceReportSrc.reports produces one source slot. Report ids or names, publisher arguments, and output_tables map by position. Report filters are applied by Salesforce before the rows are downloaded.

SOQL and report publishers use the same SalesforceSrcConn, so both can be registered in one source collection. A report incremental read needs both last_modified_column and initial_last_modified. Without them, the full report is read on each run. Returning None from the publisher means there is no new table version to publish. Tabsdata does not contact Salesforce when the collection is created. Login, object, report, field, and API-version errors appear when the function runs.

Salesforce publishers use SalesforceSrcConn to define the Salesforce login used by both connectors. conn-salesforce.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.salesforce:SalesforceSrcConn spec: credentials: kind: salesforceTokenCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:SalesforceToken spec: username: 'secret:integration@acme.com' password: 'secret:example-password' security_token: 'secret:exampleSecurityToken00' credentials:SalesforceTokenrequired instance_url:stroptional category:stroptional objects:list[str]optional entity_whitelist:list[str]optional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A publisher is registered in a source collection, and a source collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type salesforce-sosql-in --file conn-salesforce.yaml Edit the template file with the Salesforce connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-salesforce.yaml tdk collection create --name salesforce_in --conn-file conn-salesforce.yaml Then register the publisher in the collection: tdk fn register --coll salesforce_in --path publish_accounts.py::publish_accounts The collection goes in the sources group, because the connection is a source connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be sources. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: SalesforceSrc or SalesforceReportSrc for a collection created with SalesforceSrcConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name salesforce_in --conn-file conn-salesforce.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project. The template type can be salesforce-sosql-in or salesforce-report-in. Both write the same SalesforceSrcConn, so a collection created from either holds both kinds of publisher.

credentials​ A SalesforceToken with the username, password and security_token of the Salesforce user. instance_url​ An explicit instance URL. It must be an https:// URL on a Salesforce domain (salesforce.com, force.com, cloudforce.com or salesforce-setup.com). Accepts secret: too. category and objects​ Hints for entity discovery. category is a category name. objects is a non-empty list of Salesforce object API names, each 1 to 80 characters, starting with a letter, optionally ending in __c or __r. Only one of the two can be set. entity_whitelist​ A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out. conn_cfg​ Optional connector configuration.

The Snowflake connector lets Tabsdata write tables into Snowflake. Snowflake is destination-only: there is no publisher-side connector for reading from Snowflake. The SnowflakeDest connector can be used by a subscriber function to write data from a Tabsdata table into Snowflake. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a SnowflakeDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The Snowflake account is reachable from the Tabsdata server. The configured role can use the warehouse, database, and schema, and can create or write the destination tables. If stage is set, the configured role can use that permanent stage. If it is left out, the connector creates a session-scoped temporary stage.

For merge writes, schema evolution, and retry watermarks, see Merging into SQL destinations. Configure SnowflakeDest as the destination of a subscriber function to define which tables Tabsdata writes in Snowflake. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.snowflake import SnowflakeDest @subscriber( destination=SnowflakeDest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:stroptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Defines the destination tables the subscriber writes to in Snowflake. Each element in tables represents one destination slot and maps positionally to a value returned by the subscriber function. Each name is a 1-, 2-, or 3-part name (table, schema.table, or database.schema.table); double-quote a part for a case-sensitive or special-character name. if_table_exists​ "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and requires a merge_cfg list. See Merge configuration for a complete example. Controls what happens when the destination table already exists. "append" (the default) adds rows. "replace" issues TRUNCATE before COPY INTO, so the existing schema is preserved. dest_cfg​ Sets additional destination configuration. Supported keys include snowflake.logging_level and snowflake.schema_evolution_engine. Merge mode requires snowflake.schema_evolution_engine="iceberg".

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the subscriber function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" adds rows. "replace" truncates before COPY INTO, so the existing table definition stays in place. "merge" applies inserts, updates, and deletes by key and needs merge_cfg.

A one-part table name uses the connection's database and schema. Two- and three-part names override one or both defaults. Replace mode preserves the existing schema. Change the table separately before returning columns that it does not accept. Tabsdata does not connect to Snowflake when the collection is created. Account, role, warehouse, stage, and permission errors appear when the subscriber runs.

Snowflake subscribers use SnowflakeDestConn to define the account, credentials, and default namespace used by the subscriber. conn-snowflake.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.snowflake:SnowflakeDestConn spec: account: 'ABCDEFG-XY12345' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_svc' password: 'secret:CorrectHorseBatteryStaple' account:strrequired credentials:UserPasswordrequired role:stroptional database:stroptional schema:stroptional warehouse:stroptional stage:stroptional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type snowflake-bulk-out --file conn-snowflake.yaml Edit the template file with the Snowflake connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-snowflake.yaml tdk collection create --name snowflake_out --conn-file conn-snowflake.yaml Then register the subscriber in the collection: tdk fn register --coll snowflake_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders The collection goes in the destinations group, because the connection is a destination connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be destinations. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: SnowflakeDest for a collection created with SnowflakeDestConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name snowflake_out --conn-file conn-snowflake.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

account​ The Snowflake account identifier or locator, such as ABCDEFG-XY12345. credentials​ The Snowflake credentials used to authenticate. UserPassword requires a user and password; a personal access token can be passed as the password. role​ An optional role the connection runs USE for before writing. database​ The default database. Required when schema is set. schema​ The default schema. Requires database to be set. warehouse​ An optional warehouse the connection runs USE WAREHOUSE for. USE WAREHOUSE is only issued when this is set. stage​ An optional permanent stage used for PUT and COPY INTO. When unset, the plugin creates a session-scoped temporary stage instead. conn_cfg​ Optional connector-config overrides, forwarded to snowflake-connector-python.

The StarRocks connector lets Tabsdata Subscribers write data from Tabsdata Tables into StarRocks. The connector stages the data as Parquet files in cloud storage, then loads it into StarRocks through its native FILES() table function. Destination tables in StarRocks must already exist as the connector does not create them automatically. See the full subscriber walkthrough The subscriber is registered in a collection created with a StarRocksDestConn connection. The connection, and how to create the collection, are described in Connection, at the end of this page.

The StarRocks frontend is reachable from the Tabsdata server. Every destination table already exists. The connector cannot infer its key model or distribution strategy. Tabsdata can write to the staging location and StarRocks can read the staged Parquet files. The StarRocks user can insert into the destination tables and truncate them when replace mode is used.

Configure StarRocksDest as the destination of a Subscriber Function. Each returned frame maps to one entry in tables, in order. write_orders.py from tabsdatak.api import subscriber from tabsdatak.conn.starrocks import StarRocksDest @subscriber( destination=StarRocksDest( tables=[ "orders", ], ), input_tables=["sales/orders"], ) def write_orders(orders): return orders tables:list[str]required if_table_exists:stroptional schema_evolution:stroptional dest_cfg:dictoptional

tables​ Names of existing StarRocks tables, one per returned frame. Names can be table or database.table; an unqualified name uses the Connection's database. Backtick-quote individual name parts containing special characters. Create the destination tables before running the Subscriber. StarRocks table creation requires a physical layout, including a key definition and distribution strategy, that the connector cannot infer from a frame. if_table_exists​ "append" (the default) inserts rows into the existing table. "replace" truncates the existing table and then inserts the returned rows. Neither mode creates a missing table. schema_evolution​ "strict" (the default) rejects schema changes. "iceberg" applies Iceberg-style schema changes to the existing destination table; it does not change the destination into an Iceberg table. dest_cfg​ Optional destination configuration. The supported key is starrocks.logging_level.

Each entry in tables is one destination slot and maps by position to a value returned by the Subscriber Function. Returning None for a slot skips that write. if_table_exists="append" inserts rows into the existing table. "replace" truncates it first. Neither mode creates a missing table. schema_evolution="strict" rejects schema changes. "iceberg" applies supported Iceberg-style changes to the StarRocks table; it does not turn the table into an Iceberg table.

Writes are staged as Parquet, then loaded through StarRocks FILES(). S3 and Azure staging use one credential set. GCS needs service-account JSON for the upload and HMAC credentials for StarRocks's S3-compatible read. Tabsdata does not contact StarRocks or the staging service when the collection is created. Those checks happen when the subscriber runs.

StarRocksDestConn defines the StarRocks frontend address, database credentials, and cloud staging location. Register the Connection on the Collection where the Subscriber runs. conn-starrocks.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.starrocks:StarRocksDestConn spec: host: 'starrocks-fe.internal' credentials: kind: userPasswordCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:UserPassword spec: user: 'secret:tabsdata_writer' password: 'secret:example-password' staging: kind: starRocksS3Location apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.starrocks:S3Location spec: bucket: 'acme-staging' region: 'us-east-1' credentials: kind: awsAccessSecretKeyCredentials apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdatak.conn.common.types:AwsAccessSecretKey spec: access_key_id: 'secret:example-access-key' secret_access_key: 'secret:example-secret-key' base_path: '/starrocks' host:strrequired port:stroptional database:stroptional credentials:UserPasswordrequired staging:CloudLocationrequired entity_whitelist:list[str]optional conn_cfg:dictoptional

A subscriber is registered in a destination collection, and a destination collection is created with its connection. Every function registered in the collection uses that connection. Generate a connection template, which lists all the connection fields: tdk connection template --type starrocks-bulk-out --file conn-starrocks.yaml Edit the template file with the StarRocks connection information, check it, and create the collection with it: tdk connection validate --file conn-starrocks.yaml tdk collection create --name starrocks_out --conn-file conn-starrocks.yaml Then register the subscriber in the collection: tdk fn register --coll starrocks_out --path write_orders.py::write_orders The collection goes in the destinations group, because the connection is a destination connection. --group can be left out; if it is given, it must be destinations. secret:<value> gives a secret value in the file itself. $secret:<ENV_VAR> reads it from an environment variable when the collection is created, so the value never appears in the file. Either way, Tabsdata stores the secret separately, and the stored connection only shows a placeholder. Functions in the collection must use the connector of its connection: StarRocksDest for a collection created with StarRocksDestConn. Transformers go in a collection of their own. To change the connection later, for example to rotate a password, run tdk collection update --name starrocks_out --conn-file conn-starrocks.yaml. The connector cannot change; to use another one, create another collection. Creating a source or destination collection requires permission to manage the project.

host, port, and database​ host identifies the StarRocks frontend. port is the MySQL-protocol port, from 1 to 65535, and defaults to "9030". database defaults to "default" and supplies the database for unqualified destination table names. These fields accept strings or secret references. credentials​ A UserPassword containing the StarRocks username and password. Cloud storage credentials are configured separately under staging. staging​ Use one of the location classes from tabsdatak.conn.starrocks: Location Required fields Credentials S3Location bucket, region, credentials AwsAccessSecretKey AzBlobLocation container, credentials AzureAccountKey GCSLocation bucket, credentials, hmac_credentials GCPJson for uploads and GCPHmac for StarRocks reads Tabsdata must be able to upload the staged files, and StarRocks must be able to read them. For GCS, both credential types are required: uploads use the native GCS API, while StarRocks reads through the S3-compatible endpoint. Each location accepts base_path, which defaults to /, and an optional cfg dictionary for storage-client configuration. A non-root base_path starts with /, has no trailing /, and contains no empty path segments. entity_whitelist​ A YAML list of regular expressions, not a comma-separated string. It is checked to be a list of valid regular expressions, but it has no effect yet. Leave it out. conn_cfg​ Optional connector configuration overrides.

A trigger configures when a function runs. There are four ways a function can be fired: Manually When you run it Run it yourself with tdk fn trigger. This is the default for publishers, which have no input tables to fire them. On a schedule At set times A cron schedule fires the function at set times, whether or not anything upstream has changed. On new data When an input Table receives new data The function fires whenever an upstream table it depends on gets a new version. Watch every table it reads, or narrow it to a specific set. On a stream batch When a batch of streamed data is due A stream publisher takes no trigger_by at all. It fires each time a stream worker, such as SQL CDC or Kafka, hands over a batch. See Working with Triggers for how to configure each mode in code.

No matter which trigger fires a function, Tabsdata doesn't run just that one function. It follows the data dependencies and builds an execution plan: the graph of every function that must run as a result, in the correct order, across collections. There is no orchestration for you to wire up.
Every table in an execution plan stays in sync, because new data is only committed if every function in the plan succeeds. A partial failure commits nothing.

An execution plan is the Directed Acyclic Graph that Tabsdata automatically builds whenever a function is triggered. Rather than running only the function you triggered, Tabsdata follows the data dependencies to work out every other function that has to run as a result, and puts them in the order those dependencies require. A single plan can cross several collections.

A plan is a directed acyclic graph. Each node is a function, and each edge is a table that one function writes and another reads. So when you trigger a publisher, Tabsdata runs that publisher first, then runs every transformer that reads the tables it produced, and keeps working downstream until it reaches the subscribers.

Tabsdata works the edges out from the tables each function already declares. A publisher writes to its output tables, a transformer reads tables and writes others, and a subscriber reads tables and writes outside the server. Wherever one function's output table is another function's input table, the second function depends on the first, and that is the edge Tabsdata walks when it builds the plan. The event that sets this in motion is a table commit. A transformer or subscriber is triggered by a commit to any of its input tables unless trigger_by narrows it to a specific set, and because every function commits to its own output tables when it finishes, those commits trigger whatever reads them in turn. That cascade is how a single trigger becomes a plan covering many functions. See Triggers for how to configure which tables count. One consequence worth knowing: a commit does not necessarily mean the data changed. A publisher that writes three tables commits to all three every time it runs, whether or not any of them ended up different, and dependents fire on the commit rather than on a diff.

Execution plans are 100% deterministic. Before anything runs, Tabsdata fixes and records both the graph itself and the exact table versions each function will read and write, so the same starting point always produces the same plan over the same data.

A plan nests three levels below itself, and each level is where a different question gets answered: a transaction is what commits, a function run is one function executing, and a worker is the process doing the work. A function is triggered creates Execution planOne per function triggered TransactionsOne per collection in the execution plan Function runsOne per function in the transaction WorkersOne per attempted code execution (max 3)
documents.s: What a plan is made of

documents.t: Four commands cover the four levels: tdk plan, tdk trx, tdk fnrun, and tdk worker. See the CLI Guide for what each one accepts. Execution & Triggers covers what fires a plan in the first place, along with the pristine-state guarantee it carries.

A Function Run represents a single execution of a Function in Tabsdata. Whenever a Function is executed as part of an Execution Plan, Tabsdata creates a Function Run to track that individual execution. If an Execution Plan contains multiple Functions, each Function gets its own Function Run. Function Runs allow Tabsdata to track the execution of each Function independently, including its status, logs, inputs, outputs, and the Worker responsible for executing it.

An Execution Plan describes the set of Functions that need to run and the order in which they need to run. Function Runs represent the individual executions that take place within that plan. For example, an Execution Plan containing a Publisher, Transformer, and Subscriber would create a separate Function Run for each Function: Execution Plan ├── Publisher Function Run ├── Transformer Function Run └── Subscriber Function Run This makes it possible to see the status of each individual Function rather than only whether the Execution Plan as a whole succeeded or failed.
documents.s: Function Runs in an Execution Plan

documents.t: Function Runs are executed by Workers. When a Function is ready to run, Tabsdata assigns its Function Run to a Worker. The Worker performs the actual processing required by the Function and reports the status of the Function Run back to Tabsdata. This separation allows multiple Function Runs to be processed independently and, when possible, in parallel. In case of failures, function runs can be assigned to new workers and retried.

The data produced by a Function Run is written as part of a Transaction. A successful Function Run can produce changes to one or more Tables, but those changes do not become available simply because the Function Run finished. They become available when the Transaction containing those changes is committed. This allows Tabsdata to keep the execution of an individual Function separate from the process of publishing its output.

Each Function Run has its own status throughout its execution. This makes Function Runs useful for understanding where an Execution Plan is currently running or where a failure occurred. If one Function fails in a plan containing several Functions, you can identify the specific Function Run that failed and inspect its logs without treating the Execution Plan as a single unit.

Because each Function execution is tracked as its own Function Run, Tabsdata can operate on individual runs after they have been created. A failed Function Run can be recovered, allowing Tabsdata to retry that execution without starting the entire workflow again. A completed Function Run can also be replayed, allowing the Function to execute again using the same inputs. Functions can be replayed even if the source data the function relies on has changed.

Function Runs can be inspected through the TDK to view their status, logs, and other execution information. For example, you can view the logs produced by a specific Function Run: tdk fnrun logs --fnrun FNRUN Or retrieve information about the Function Run itself: tdk fnrun get --fnrun FNRUN See the CLI Guide for the complete set of commands for inspecting, recovering, and replaying Function Runs.

Tabsdata publishes the output of an execution plan only once every function in that plan has succeeded. This guarantee is called pristine state, and it is why a failed run leaves your tables reading exactly as they did before it started. Execution & Triggers describes the guarantee in full. A transaction is the unit Tabsdata uses to enforce it, and Tabsdata draws the boundary at the collection.

A collection holds the connections, functions, and tables for one step of a workflow. Tabsdata creates one transaction for every collection an execution plan touches, and commits all the tables it changed in that collection at the same moment. Anyone querying the collection therefore sees either the whole of the plan's output or none of it.
documents.s: The collection is the commit boundary

documents.t: An execution plan can span several collections, and Tabsdata commits each one under its own transaction, so a single plan normally has more than one. This is what makes a plan multi-transactional, and it means the commit boundaries follow the collection boundaries your workflow already has.

tdk trx works the same way as tdk plan, except that you identify a transaction with --trx instead of --plan: $ tdk trx list [--status R] [--coll C] [--fn F] $ tdk trx get --trx TRX See the CLI Guide for the full set of commands and the status codes each accepts.

A worker is the process that executes the code defined in a Tabsdata Function Each worker runs as an isolated process on the Tabsdata server's Kubernetes cluster. Performance optimizations such as Polars Streaming and Lazy Evaluation allow workers to process datasets incrementally, allowing them to handle datasets larger than the memory available on the machine's hardware.

Tabsdata deploys one worker for each execution attempt of the function code. If a worker fails, Tabsdata snapshots the worker's execution log and spins up a new worker to retry the execution. By default, a function run will attempt three executions before stalling. A function is triggered Function runGenerated by the trigger Worker 1Failed Worker 2Failed Worker 3Succeeded Three workers is the default limit. Had the third one failed as well, the function run would stall instead of starting a fourth.
A worker is where a function's output ends up, so its logs are the first place to look when a function run fails: $ tdk worker logs --worker WID Pass --file - to write the log to stdout.
You can retry a single worker without re-running the whole plan: $ tdk worker recover --worker WID

tdk worker list filters down from any level of the plan, so you can start from whichever identifier you already have: $ tdk worker list [--status R] [--coll C] [--fn F] [--plan P] [--trx T] [--fnrun FR] See the CLI Guide for the full set of commands and the status codes each accepts.

A Tabsdata Function is Tabsdata's operational unit of work and defines a single step that reads data from or writes data to a Tabsdata Table. Tabsdata Functions build on the familiar model of a regular Python function, where data comes in through a parameter, the function performs work on that parameter, and the result is returned through the return statement. Tabsdata extends this model to data integration by abstracting data sources and destinations into the simple parameters and return statement of a Python function. Users define their inputs, which can be a SQL query against a database, a file in object storage, or a Tabsdata Table. They then define where they want the output data to be written, whether that is a database table, a file in object storage, or another Tabsdata Table. Tabsdata handles retrieving, converting, and moving the data between those systems. While the data is being passed through the Function, Tabsdata materializes it as a DataFrame object that users can transform through an expression-based API. This allows users to work with tabular data independently of where it is physically stored or how it needs to be moved between systems. PublisherTransformerSubscriber Publisher: Database to Python to Tabsdata Table.@td.publisher(input=database,output=['orders'],)def clean_orders(orders):cleaned = ...return cleanedDatabaseTabsdata Tableorders

There are three types of Tabsdata functions: publishers: read data from external systems and publish data into Tabsdata Tables transformers: read data from Tabsdata Tables and write data into Tabsdata Tables subscribers: read data from Tabsdata Tables and subscribe data into Tabsdata Tables Publishers External SystemTabsdata Table Reads an external system and writes Tabsdata Tables. Transformers Tabsdata TableTabsdata Table Reads Tabsdata Tables and writes new Tabsdata Tables. Subscribers Tabsdata TableExternal System Reads Tabsdata Tables and writes an external system.

The decorator maps declared inputs to the Python callable's parameters. It also maps returned values to output Tables or to destination slots in an external system. The number and order of parameters and returned values must match the corresponding declarations. Publishers and Subscribers use a Connector for the system-specific read or write operation. The Collection's Connection supplies the configuration and credentials used by that Connector. Transformers work entirely with Tabsdata Tables and do not use an external Connection. Output Tables belong to the Collection where the Function is registered. Input Table references can identify Tables in other Collections within the same Project, allowing Functions to connect into a larger workflow.

A Trigger determines when a Function starts. A Transformer or Subscriber without trigger_by runs whenever one of its input Tables commits a new version. A Publisher has no input Tables, so without trigger_by it runs only when triggered manually. Set trigger_by to a schedule, or to one or more Table references, to control what starts the Function.

Registration sends the Function definition, source code, and required bundle metadata to the Server. A Function name must be unique within its Collection. Register a decorated callable from a Python file with: tdk fn register --coll <collection_name> --path <path_to_python_file>::<function_name> Pass --update when the same command should update an existing Function with that name. Registration records the definition; it does not execute the Function. See Register a Function for the full procedure.

A manual Trigger can start any registered Function: tdk fn trigger --coll <collection_name> --name <function_name> The Server evaluates the Function's dependencies and creates an Execution Plan. Each Function included in that plan gets a Function Run, and a Worker executes each attempt. A successful run that produces Tables creates new Table Versions; the Server keeps the registered Function definition after the Worker exits. Function code does not run in the CLI process that sends the command. The CLI requests the Trigger, while the Server coordinates and records the execution.

A publisher reads data from an external system and publishes it to Tabsdata tables. Each run reads the source, calls the function, and commits the returned tables together. Unlike a stream publisher, a regular publisher does not keep reading. It reads the source only when it runs. The publisher must be registered in a source collection whose connection matches the source.

publisher( source, output_tables, trigger_by=None, on_tables=None, ) Parameter Type source Src required output_tables list[str] required trigger_by CronTrigger | TablesTrigger optional on_tables list[OnTablesAction] optional source​ The source to read. The source class decides what is read and how many slots are passed to the function. A SQL source has one slot per query. A file source can read several files into one slot. The source does not contain the server address or credentials. Those come from the connection of the collection where the publisher is registered. The page for each connector lists its source classes and settings. output_tables​ A non-empty list of local table names, one for each value the function returns. A name must start with a letter, use only letters, numbers, and underscores, and be no longer than 64 characters. The source slot count and output table count do not have to match. A publisher can combine several source slots into one table or derive several tables from one slot. trigger_by​ The trigger that starts the publisher automatically: a CronTrigger or TablesTrigger. Without trigger_by, the publisher runs only when triggered manually. See Execution & Triggers. on_tables​ Actions to run on the output tables after the publisher succeeds, such as data quality checks.

Returning None for a Table leaves its current version unchanged.

A publisher function has one parameter per source slot and returns one frame per output table. Parameters. Source slots are passed to the function in source order. Annotate a parameter as TableFrameSpec for one frame or TableFramesSpec for a list of frames. A slot can be None when there is no batch for it. Context. The function can have a final ctx: TrxCtx parameter. Use ctx to keep values between successful runs. For example, an incremental SQL publisher can save its last processed ID with ctx.set_attr() and use it in the next query. Return value. Return values map to output_tables in order. One output can be returned on its own; several outputs are returned as a tuple. Returning None for one output leaves that table's current version unchanged. Slot counts. The number of source slots does not have to match the number of output tables. The function can combine several inputs into one table or create several tables from one input. Tabsdata checks the slot counts and function signature when the publisher is registered.

All publishers in a source collection use the same connection. Each publisher has its own source settings, code, and output tables. The connection is created with the collection. Updating a connection changes how every publisher in that collection reaches the external system.

Register. tdk fn register uploads the publisher. Its collection and connection must already exist. Run. A manual, cron, or table trigger starts a transaction. The source is read before the function runs. Commit. A successful run commits the output tables together. Each commit adds a table version. Update. tdk fn update replaces the code and decorator settings. Delete. Deleting the function stops future runs but does not delete its output tables or their versions. For step-by-step guides on building a publisher for a specific external system, see Publishers under How-to Guides.

When source data changes, a Subscriber Function may need to update or delete records already written to the destination, as well as insert new records. To do so, Tabsdata supports merge writes. Users specify key columns to match records and an operation column that tells Tabsdata whether to insert, update, or delete each row. The Subscriber returns the changes, and the connector applies them to the destination table. Merge writes are supported by the Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks connectors.

To configure a merge, set if_table_exists="merge" on the destination and pass a merge_cfg list containing the key and operation columns for each table. For example, this Subscriber reads order changes from Tabsdata and applies them to ORDERS in Snowflake: from tabsdatak.api import subscriber, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.conn.snowflake import MergeCfg, SnowflakeDest @subscriber( destination=SnowflakeDest( tables=["ORDERS"], if_table_exists="merge", merge_cfg=[MergeCfg(on=["order_id"], op_column="op")], schema_evolution="update", dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}, ), input_tables=["capture/order_changes"], ) def load_orders(changes: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return changes Here, on=["order_id"] matches records by order ID, while op_column="op" identifies the column containing the operation. The Function returns the changes from capture/order_changes for the connector to write. Because a Subscriber can write to several tables, the MergeCfg entries must follow the order of tables, and both lists must have the same length. Use a list even for a single table. The merge_cfg setting is required for merge writes and cannot be used with other write modes. The on setting requires at least one key column, and those columns must exist in both the incoming data and the destination when the merge runs. If several columns form the key, all their values must match. MergeCfg is imported from the same connector module as the destination. For Snowflake and BigQuery, merge writes also require an Iceberg schema evolution setting in dest_cfg, as described under Schema evolution.

After matching records by key, Tabsdata uses the operation column to decide what to write. In the example above, op accepts these values: Marker Operation i Insert the row if its key does not exist in the destination. u Update the row matching its key. d Delete the row matching its key. An insert leaves an existing record unchanged, while an update or delete does nothing if the record is missing. Uppercase I, U, and D are also accepted, but spaces are not removed, so " d " is invalid. Tabsdata removes rows with invalid or null operations before processing the batch. Because the operation column is used to control the write, Tabsdata excludes it when creating the destination table or updating its schema.

A record may change several times within the same batch. Tabsdata combines changes with the same key before writing them, using the first and last valid operations to determine the result. These operations follow the row order in the materialized batch, so the order returned by the Function matters: First operation Last operation Result Insert Insert or update Insert using the latest row. Insert Delete No destination write for this key. Update or delete Insert or update Update using the latest row. Update or delete Delete Delete the matching record. For example, i → u → d → i inserts the latest row because the final change adds the record again. With i → u → d, nothing is written because the record was created and deleted in the same batch. For a delete, Tabsdata keeps the data from the last insert or update for that key, or the first row if all operations are deletes. This allows delete records to contain just the key columns and operation. The destination therefore receives the combined change, without storing the intermediate changes as history.

If the destination table does not exist, all three connectors can create it from the staged data's schema, excluding the operation column. The database and schema or dataset must already exist, and the Connection must have the required permissions. For existing tables, Snowflake and BigQuery write columns shared by the incoming data and the destination. Updates leave the keys unchanged, while inserts include them. Columns found only in the destination are left unchanged on updates and omitted from inserts, where the destination's defaults and constraints apply. For columns found only in the incoming data, schema_evolution="strict" excludes them from the write. Values written to shared columns must still satisfy the destination's types and constraints. Databricks handles column matching through Delta's merge rules. With strict, it uses UPDATE SET * and INSERT *, while update enables schema evolution and excludes the operation column. The operation marker should therefore use a separate column from the data being written.

Incoming data may contain new columns or values too large for the destination's current column types. Schema evolution controls whether Tabsdata can change the table to accept that data. Set schema_evolution on the destination to choose the behavior. All three destinations default to "strict" in Tabsdata 2.1.0: Setting Behavior "strict" Does not add or widen data columns on an existing table. A configured watermark column is an exception. "update" Allows new data columns and supported type widening. For Snowflake and BigQuery, the connector uses an Iceberg schema evolution engine to compare the incoming and destination schemas. This engine must be configured for merge writes even when schema_evolution="strict": # SnowflakeDest dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"} # BigQueryDest dest_cfg={"bigquery.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"} When schema_evolution="update", the engine uses that comparison to apply supported changes through ALTER TABLE. The Iceberg setting controls how schemas are compared; it does not convert the destination into an Apache Iceberg table. Databricks uses Delta's MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION for schema_evolution="update", so it does not require a schema_evolution_engine setting. On each merge, Tabsdata also sets the destination table's delta.enableTypeWidening property to true for update or false for strict.

Type widening allows a column to store larger values, such as longer strings or numbers with greater precision. The supported changes depend on the destination: Destination Supported widening Snowflake Wider VARCHAR lengths and greater NUMBER precision at the same scale. The connector does not widen between different base types. BigQuery Supported numeric promotions, including INT64 → NUMERIC → BIGNUMERIC → FLOAT64, and wider type parameters. Databricks Type changes supported by Delta type widening. Setting schema_evolution="update" allows these supported changes. If the incoming data requires a conversion outside these rules, the write can still fail.

A Subscriber may retry a write after data has already reached the destination. To recognize these retries, Tabsdata can store the Transaction ID in a watermark column. If that ID is already in the table, Tabsdata skips the write. Set watermark_column on the destination to enable this check: SnowflakeDest( tables=["ORDERS"], if_table_exists="merge", merge_cfg=[MergeCfg(on=["order_id"], op_column="op")], watermark_column="wm", dest_cfg={"snowflake.schema_evolution_engine": "iceberg"}, ) The configured name applies to all tables listed in the destination. If the column is missing, Tabsdata adds it even when schema_evolution="strict". Existing rows have NULL in the new column, while inserted and updated rows receive the current Transaction ID. The watermark name must differ from the key columns and operation column, following the destination's rules for uppercase and lowercase names. Watermarks work with append and merge, but not with replace. Retries use the same Transaction ID, while new Transactions have different IDs and write normally. The check depends on a matching ID remaining in the destination. A batch containing only deletes leaves no new watermark value.

The connectors differ in how they stage data, change schemas, and match column names: Behavior Snowflake BigQuery Databricks Staging Snowflake stage, then a temporary table GCS, then a temporary table Unity Catalog volume, then a temporary staging table Schema changes under update Connector applies ALTER TABLE using Iceberg schema comparison Connector applies ALTER TABLE using Iceberg schema comparison Delta merge schema evolution Required merge setting snowflake.schema_evolution_engine="iceberg" bigquery.schema_evolution_engine="iceberg" No engine setting Column names Unquoted names resolve as uppercase; double quotes preserve case Case-insensitive; backticks quote names Case-insensitive; backticks quote names For example, Snowflake resolves an unquoted order_id as uppercase, so on=["order_id"] matches a stored ORDER_ID column. BigQuery and Databricks match column names without considering case, including when those names are quoted. BigQuery also requires destination table names to be enclosed in backticks, as in tables=["`orders`"].

Tabsdata checks the configuration before writing and validates the incoming data during execution. The following conditions can cause the merge to fail: Condition Result Merge mode without merge_cfg, or merge_cfg without merge mode Configuration error. merge_cfg is not a list, or its length differs from tables Configuration error. Empty on, or an operation column that matches a key Configuration error. Snowflake or BigQuery merge without the required Iceberg engine setting Configuration error. A watermark with replace, or a watermark name that matches a key or operation column Configuration error. Missing operation or key columns in the incoming batch Runtime error. No shared data columns between the batch and destination Runtime error. Several incoming columns match the same configured column name Runtime error. For field definitions, see the MergeCfg API reference for Snowflake, BigQuery, and Databricks.

A stream publisher reads data continuously from a stream source, such as a CDC log or a Kafka topic, and publishes it into Tabsdata tables in batches. A regular publisher runs when it is triggered and reads what is in the source at that moment. A stream publisher has no trigger. Registering it starts a worker that keeps reading the source, collects what it reads, and runs the function once per batch. The batch_* parameters of @stream_publisher decide when a batch is complete. These sources work with @stream_publisher: Source Reads Page PostgresCdcStreamSrc Postgres changes, from the WAL Postgres CDC MySQLCdcStreamSrc MySQL changes, from the binlog MySQL CDC Db2CdcStreamSrc Db2 changes, from the SQL Replication CD tables Db2 CDC KafkaStreamSrc Messages from Kafka topics Kafka All of them use the batch parameters described on this page.
