stream_sales_changes.py from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat @stream_publisher( source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc( tables=["public.orders", "public.customers"], replication_slot="tabsdata_sales", start_from="full", ), output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], batch_max_secs=300, batch_max_rows=50_000, ) def stream_sales_changes( orders: TableFramesSpec, customers: TableFramesSpec, ) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: return concat(orders), concat(customers) source is the stream source. Its connection comes from the collection the function is registered in, as for any publisher. output_tables are the Tabsdata tables the function writes, in the order the function returns them. batch_max_secs and batch_max_rows decide when a batch is handed to the function: here, every 5 minutes, or sooner once 50,000 changes are waiting, but never more often than once a minute. The function receives one parameter per source slot. Each parameter is a list of frames: the data read for that slot since the previous batch. concat combines them into one frame.

stream_publisher( source, output_tables, *, batch_min_secs=None, batch_max_secs=None, batch_max_rows=None, batch_max_bytes=None, batch_idle_secs=None, on_tables=None, flush_interval_mins=None, ) Parameter Type source StreamSrc required output_tables list[str] required batch_min_secs int optional batch_max_secs int optional batch_max_rows int optional batch_max_bytes int optional batch_idle_secs int optional on_tables list[OnTablesAction] optional flush_interval_mins int deprecated source and output_tables can be given by position or by name. The other parameters must be given by name. source​ The stream source to read: one of the sources in the table above. output_tables​ The tables the function writes, as a non-empty list of table names. The number of output tables does not have to match the number of source slots. on_tables​ Actions to run on the output tables, such as data quality checks, as for a regular publisher.

A batch is everything the worker has read since the previous batch. Each batch runs the function once, and the function's output tables are committed together: every batch adds one version to each output table. Parameter Default Description batch_min_secs 60 The shortest time between two batches, in seconds. Never less than 60. batch_max_secs none Seconds after the previous batch at which data that is waiting is handed to the function. batch_max_rows none Rows waiting that make a batch due. batch_max_bytes none Bytes waiting that make a batch due. batch_idle_secs none Seconds after the previous batch at which, if no data is waiting, the function runs with an empty batch. At least one of batch_max_secs, batch_max_rows and batch_max_bytes is required.

The worker checks after every read from the source. Counting from the previous batch (or from when the worker started): When data is waiting, a batch is due once batch_min_secs have passed and any of these is true: batch_max_secs have passed, at least batch_max_rows rows are waiting, at least batch_max_bytes bytes are waiting. When no data is waiting, nothing happens, unless batch_idle_secs is set. Once batch_idle_secs have passed, the function runs with an empty batch. As a result: batch_min_secs is a floor for every other setting. If 50,000 rows arrive 10 seconds after a batch, they wait until batch_min_secs have passed, and more rows keep joining them in the meantime. batch_max_rows and batch_max_bytes make a batch due; they do not cap its size. A batch holds everything that is waiting when it closes, which can be more than the threshold. Rows and bytes are counted over all the slots of the source together, not per table. For a CDC source, one row is one change. Bytes are approximate: the size of the data files already written plus an estimate of what is still in memory. batch_max_secs counts from the previous batch, not from when the data arrived. After a quiet period longer than batch_max_secs, the first data to arrive is handed over right away. Batches are processed one at a time, in order. Tabsdata looks for new batches about every 30 seconds, so a batch can start up to that long after it is due. If the function takes longer than the batch interval, batches queue up and are processed in turn.
documents.s: When a batch is handed to the function

documents.t: The batch parameters are checked when the function is decorated. A violation raises error API_29: batch_min_secs, batch_max_secs and batch_idle_secs must be whole numbers of seconds, at least 60. batch_max_rows and batch_max_bytes must be whole numbers, at least 1. batch_max_secs must be at least batch_min_secs. batch_idle_secs must be at least batch_max_secs, or, without batch_max_secs, at least batch_min_secs. At least one of batch_max_secs, batch_max_rows and batch_max_bytes must be set.

Goal Parameters Result Steady, bounded latency batch_max_secs=120 A batch every 2 minutes while data arrives. Size first, with a time bound batch_max_rows=100_000, batch_max_secs=900 A batch as soon as 100,000 rows are waiting, and at least every 15 minutes. Large batches, few runs batch_min_secs=600, batch_max_secs=3600 At most one batch every 10 minutes, and at least one an hour while data arrives. Runs even when the source is quiet batch_max_secs=300, batch_idle_secs=3600 A batch every 5 minutes while data arrives, and an empty run every hour when nothing arrives, for example to keep downstream functions on a schedule.

Stream sources also have buffer settings in their src_cfg, such as tabsdata.cdc.buffer.max_rows or tabsdata.kafka.buffer.max_rows. Buffer settings and batch parameters work at different levels: Buffer settings decide when the worker writes what it has read from memory to a data file. They bound the worker's memory. Batch parameters decide when the files written so far, and anything still in memory, are handed to the function as one batch. Most streams only need the batch parameters. The buffer settings of each source are listed on its connector page.

stream_sales_changes.py 1from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, TableFramesSpec, stream_publisher 2from tabsdatak.conn.postgres import PostgresCdcStreamSrc 3from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import concat 4 5 1@stream_publisher( 2 source=PostgresCdcStreamSrc( 3 tables=["public.orders", "public.customers"], 9 replication_slot="tabsdata_sales", 10 start_from="full", 11 ), 4 output_tables=["orders_changes", "customers_changes"], 5 batch_max_secs=300, 14 batch_max_rows=50_000, 15) 67def stream_sales_changes( 17 orders: TableFramesSpec, 18 customers: TableFramesSpec, 19) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec, TableFrameSpec]: 8 return concat(orders), concat(customers) 1Function decorator Defines the stream source, output Tables, and the conditions that make a batch due. 2Stream source Reads changes continuously from Postgres. The Collection's Connection provides the server address and credentials. 3Source slots Each tracked table is one source slot, in the order listed. 4Output tables Tabsdata Tables that receive the values returned by the function. 5Batch parameters A batch is due after five minutes or when 50,000 rows are waiting, whichever happens first after the minimum interval. 6Function body Receives one list of frames per source slot and returns one frame per output Table. 7Arguments The arguments receive the frames collected for each source slot since the previous batch. 8Return concat combines each slot's frames. The returned values map to output_tables in order.

A stream publisher function has one parameter per source slot, annotated TableFramesSpec, and returns one TableFrameSpec per output table. Slots. A CDC source has one slot per entry in its tables, in the same order. A Kafka source has a single slot. Parameters. Each parameter receives a list of frames with the data read for that slot since the previous batch. For a CDC source, the list holds at most one frame. For Kafka, it can hold several, possibly with different schemas; combine them with concat(frames, how="diagonal_relaxed") if their columns can differ. Empty batches. A slot with no new data receives an empty list. concat of an empty list returns None. Return value. A tuple with one element per output table, in the order of output_tables. With a single output table, the frame can be returned on its own. Returning None for a table means no new data: the table gets a version without data, and its previous data stays current. No other parameters. A stream publisher cannot declare a ctx parameter or any parameter beyond its slots. concat is imported from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions.

Register. tdk fn register starts the worker. The function must be registered in a source collection whose connection matches the source; see the source's connector page. Disable and enable. tdk stream disable stops the worker; tdk stream enable starts it again, from where it stopped. tdk stream list shows the stream publishers and their state. Update. tdk fn update restarts the worker with the new code and settings. It resumes from where it stopped. Delete. Deleting the function stops the worker. Check the source's connector page for anything left on the source system, such as a Postgres replication slot. Failures. If the worker fails, Tabsdata restarts it, waiting one minute after the first failure and doubling the wait after each further failure, up to 30 minutes. Start over. tdk fn update --reset-stage discards the stream's recorded position. The stream starts again as if it were new: from the source's starting position, or with a new full load for a CDC source with start_from="full". On a restart, the stream reads again whatever it had not yet handed to the function. A CDC stream publishes every change once, even across restarts. A Kafka stream is at least once: after a restart, some messages may be published again.

The full load of a CDC source (start_from="full") is not subject to the batch parameters. It is handed to the function as one batch, covering every tracked table, as soon as it has been read. If the load fails or is interrupted, it is discarded and runs again from the start. The batch parameters apply to the changes that follow.

flush_interval_mins was the only batch setting before 2.2.0. It is deprecated, and is converted to batch_max_secs = flush_interval_mins * 60, so it must be at least 1. It cannot be combined with any batch_* parameter. Doing so raises error API_30. It raises a Python DeprecationWarning when the function is decorated, and the worker logs a warning when it starts. Python hides DeprecationWarning by default, so the worker log is where the warning shows. To migrate, replace flush_interval_mins=N with batch_max_secs=N * 60.

A subscriber reads Tabsdata tables and writes to an external system. The function can filter, rename, or otherwise prepare the data before it is written. A subscriber belongs to a destination collection. That collection's connection provides the address and credentials for the destination.

subscriber( destination, input_tables, trigger_by=None, ) Parameter Type destination Dest required input_tables list[str] required trigger_by CronTrigger | TablesTrigger | AllTablesTrigger optional destination​ The destination to write to. The destination class decides where the data is written and how many slots the function must return. The destination uses the connection of the collection where the subscriber is registered. The page for each connector lists its destination classes and settings. input_tables​ A non-empty list of table references in the form [collection/]table[@versions]. Omit the collection for a table in the subscriber's collection. Use @versions to select a version, a version range, a comma-separated list, or NEW. Each entry maps to one function parameter, in list order. trigger_by​ The trigger that starts the subscriber automatically: a CronTrigger, TablesTrigger, or AllTablesTrigger. Without trigger_by, a commit to any input table triggers the subscriber. A subscriber can also be run manually. The trigger decides when the function runs. The version selector in input_tables decides which data it sends. See Execution & Triggers.

The Collection's Connection provides the address and credentials. 3Input tables Tabsdata Tables to read. This Subscriber reads vendors and items from the sales Collection. 4Function body Receives the input data and returns the data to write to MySQL. 5Arguments The vendors and items arguments receive the data from input_tables in the order listed. 6Body code Filters the vendors to include only active vendors. 7Return The returned data is written to the destination Tables in the order listed in tables. Returning None for a Table skips the write.

A subscriber function has one parameter per input table and returns one frame per destination slot. Parameters. Inputs are passed to the function in input_tables order. Each parameter is a TableFrameSpec. An input can be None when the requested upstream batch is absent. Context. The function can have a final ctx: TrxCtx parameter to keep values between successful runs. Return value. Return values map to the destination slots in destination order. One slot can be returned on its own; several slots are returned as a tuple. Returning None for a slot skips that write. Slot counts. The number of input tables does not have to match the number of destination slots. The function can combine several inputs into one write or create several destination tables from one input. Tabsdata checks the slot counts and function signature when the subscriber is registered.

All subscribers in a destination collection use the same connection. Each subscriber has its own input tables, destination settings, and code. Input tables can come from the subscriber's collection or another collection. Updating the collection's connection changes how every subscriber in that collection reaches the external system.

Register. tdk fn register uploads the subscriber. Its collection and connection must already exist. Run. A manual, scheduled, or table trigger starts a transaction and resolves the requested input versions. Write. The function's returned frames are handed to the destination. The transaction succeeds only after the destination write succeeds. Update. tdk fn update replaces the code and decorator settings. Delete. Deleting the function stops future writes. It does not remove data already written to the external system. For step-by-step guides on building a subscriber for a specific external system, see Subscribers under How-to Guides. For inserts, updates, and deletes into Snowflake, BigQuery, or Databricks, see Merging into SQL destinations.
A transformer reads Tabsdata tables, transforms their data, and writes the result back to Tabsdata. It does not read or write an external system, so it does not use a connection.

collection · world? collection · insights · data product? ▶ Trigger transformer Table country ? //world Committed Table city ? //world Committed Transformer find_big_cities ? Table big_cities ? //insights No versions yet

transformer( input_tables, output_tables, trigger_by=None, on_tables=None, ) Parameter Type input_tables list[str] required output_tables list[str] required trigger_by CronTrigger | TablesTrigger | AllTablesTrigger optional on_tables list[OnTablesAction] optional input_tables​ A non-empty list of table references in the form [collection/]table[@versions]. Omit the collection for a table in the transformer's collection. Use @versions to select a version, a version range, a comma-separated list, or NEW. Each entry maps to one function parameter. A single-version reference receives a TableFrameSpec; a reference that selects several versions receives a TableFramesSpec. output_tables​ A non-empty list of local table names, one for each value returned by the function. The output tables belong to the transformer's collection. Each name must start with a letter, contain only letters, numbers, and underscores, and be no longer than 64 characters. trigger_by​ The trigger that starts the transformer automatically: a CronTrigger, TablesTrigger, or AllTablesTrigger. Without trigger_by, a commit to any input table triggers the transformer. A transformer can also be run manually. The trigger decides when the function runs. The version selector in input_tables decides which versions it reads. See Execution & Triggers. on_tables​ Actions to run on the output tables after the transformer succeeds, such as data quality checks.

find_big_cities.py 1from tabsdatak.api import transformer, TableFrameSpec 2import tabsdatak.api.tableframe as tdf 3 4 1@transformer( 2 input_tables=["world/country", "world/city"], 3 output_tables=["big_cities"], 8) 45def find_big_cities(country: TableFrameSpec, city: TableFrameSpec) -> tuple[TableFrameSpec]: 6 countries = country.rename({"name": "country_name"}).drop( 11 ["population", "continent"] 12 ) 13 joined = city.join(countries, left_on="country_code", right_on="code") 7 return (joined.filter(tdf.col("population") > 3_000_000),) 1Function decorator Defines the input and output Tables for the Transformer. 2Input tables Tabsdata Tables to read. Use collection/table to reference a Table in another Collection. 3Output tables Tables where the transformed data is written. These belong to the Transformer's Collection. 4Function body Reads the country and city data, joins it, and returns cities with a population above three million. 5Arguments The arguments receive the data from input_tables in the order listed. An argument is None if the requested Table version does not exist. 6Body code Renames the country name column, removes unused columns, and joins the country and city data. 7Return The returned data is written to the Tables listed in output_tables, in that order. Returning None for a Table leaves its current version unchanged.

A transformer function has one parameter per input table and returns one frame per output table. Parameters. Inputs are passed to the function in input_tables order. Annotate a parameter as TableFrameSpec for one frame or TableFramesSpec for a list of frames. An input can be None when the requested upstream batch is absent. Context. The function can have a final ctx: TrxCtx parameter to keep values between successful runs. Return value. Return values map to output_tables in order. One output can be returned on its own; several outputs are returned as a tuple. Returning None for one output leaves that table's current version unchanged. Tabsdata checks the input count, output count, and function signature when the transformer is registered.

A transformer can read tables from its own collection or another collection. Its output tables are always local to the collection where the transformer is registered. Table references are resolved when a run starts. When a trigger starts a larger execution plan, Tabsdata passes the versions produced for that transaction through the plan so downstream transformers read a consistent set of data.

Register. tdk fn register uploads the transformer to its collection. No connection is required. Run. A manual, scheduled, or table trigger starts a transaction and resolves the requested input versions. Commit. A successful run commits the output tables together. Each commit adds a table version. Update. tdk fn update replaces the code and decorator settings. Delete. Deleting the function stops future runs but does not delete its output tables or their versions. For step-by-step guidance on building a transformer, see Transformers under How-to Guides.

A Group is an organizational layer inside a tabsdata project that organizes workflow steps according to their role in the workflow. By default, all tabsdata projects come with three groups: sources, default, and destinations 1. the sources group stores everything related to ingesting data from external systems 2. the default group stores everything related to transforming data inside tabsdata 3. the destinations group stores everything related to loading data into external systems Groups separate workflow resources based on type of data movementZoom in Database postgres Tabsdata Server sources Publisher load_users Table users default Transformer rank_users Table top_users destinations Subscriber sync_users Warehouse snowflake

The sources, default, and destinations groups are special groups that must exist in your workflow. They are dedicated spaces for registering publisher and subscriber functions and cannot be modified, duplicated, or removed from your project. Outside these three system groups, users can create any number of groups to organize their transformer functions.

Groups are useful for separating workflow steps that happen across tabsdata server boundaries (ingestion, load) from workflow steps that happen inside the tabsdata server (transform). Groups are also useful for separating data transformation workflow steps by the type of data transformation being done. For example, a popular data design pattern is the Medallion Architecture for Data Integration, which breaks data transformation into three layers: Bronze: Layer that ingests raw source data from external systems with the goal of having as close of a representation to data in the external system Silver: Layer that cleans, dedupes, normalizes, and joins related entities Gold: Layer that applies granular, business-specific transformations and creates "consumer-ready" tables. Users looking to implement this design pattern in tabsdata can do so with five groups within Tabsdata: two built-in groups (sources, destinations) and three custom groups (bronze, silver, gold). External systems GroupsourcesPublishers Ingest from external systems. Built in GroupbronzeTransformers Raw data, kept as close to the external system as possible. User created GroupsilverTransformers Cleaned, deduped, normalized, and joined. User created GroupgoldTransformers Business-specific transformations, consumer-ready tables. User created GroupdestinationsSubscribers Write out to external systems. Built in External systems

The Projects view in the Tabsdata UI shows how data moves between Groups, including the number of Tables, rows, and bytes moving through each stage. s3_src7,000,000 rows · 202.9 MBin 2 tablesbronze7,000,000 rows · 202.9 MBin 2 tablessilver3,739,484 rows · 122.5 MBin 1 tablegold934,871 rows · 30.6 MBin 1 tablesnowflake_out934,871 rows · 30.6 MBin 1 table

The sources, default, and destinations Groups are created with every Project. These system Groups cannot be renamed or deleted. Custom Groups can be created, renamed, and deleted within a Project. See Create a Group, Update a Group, and Delete a Group for step-by-step instructions.

Data quality checks validate the rows of a Table as a Function writes it. A check is a DataQuality object passed to a Publisher or Transformer through the on_tables argument of its decorator. After the Function succeeds, Tabsdata runs the check against the named output Table, where it can label rows, remove or copy rows that fail, write a summary, or fail the Transaction. Data quality checks are available on @publisher, @stream_publisher, and @transformer. @subscriber does not take on_tables. from tabsdatak.api import transformer, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.dataquality import ( AnyFailed, DataQuality, Filter, IsBetween, IsIn, IsNotNull, Summary, ) # transformer that dedupes the raw orders, with a data quality check that moves # rows failing any rule to orders_rejected and writes a summary of the verdicts @transformer( input_tables=["raw_orders"], output_tables=["orders"], on_tables=[ DataQuality( table="orders", classifiers=[ IsNotNull(["order_id"]), IsBetween(["amount"], min_val=0, max_val=10000), IsIn(["status"], values={"open", "shipped", "cancelled"}), ], operators=[ Filter(AnyFailed(), to_table="orders_rejected", include_quality_columns="criteria"), Summary(), ], ), ], ) def clean_orders(raw_orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return raw_orders.unique() A DataQuality check has three parts: table: the output Table the check runs on classifiers: the rules that label each row, at least one operators: what to do with the labels, at least one

A classifier evaluates one or more columns and writes a verdict for each row into a new verdict column. Classifiers fall into two kinds: boolean classifiers decide whether each value passes a rule, and categorizers assign each value to a bin.

Checks Classifiers Null and NaN IsNull, IsNotNull, IsNan, IsNotNan, IsNullOrNan, IsNotNullNorNan Sign of a number IsPositive, IsNegative, IsZero, IsNotZero, IsPositiveOrZero, IsNegativeOrZero Booleans IsTrue, IsFalse Ranges IsBetween, IsNotBetween Sets of values IsIn, IsNotIn Text Matches, DoesNotMatch, HasLength from tabsdatak.dataquality import HasLength, IsBetween, IsIn, IsNotNull, Matches IsNotNull(["order_id", "customer_id"]) IsBetween(["amount"], min_val=0, max_val=10000, closed_on="both") IsIn(["status"], values={"open", "shipped", "cancelled"}) Matches(["email"], pattern=r"^[^@]+@[^@]+$") HasLength(["country_code"], min_len=2, max_len=2) Classifiers share these settings: column_names: the columns to classify. Each entry is a column name, or a (column, verdict_column) tuple that names the verdict column. When omitted, the classifier applies to every user column. on_missing_column: "ignore" (the default) skips a named column that is not in the Table, and "fail" fails the check. on_wrong_type: "ignore" (the default) skips a column whose data type the classifier does not support, and "fail" fails the check. on_wrong_value: "ignore" (the default) gives a null verdict for a value that cannot be evaluated, and "fail" fails the check. tags: labels that scope operators to this classifier. prefix: text added to the start of every verdict column name. Defaults to @td.dq., and "" adds no prefix.

ScaleCategorizer assigns each numeric value to a bin of a scale. The verdict column holds the bin number, or a reserved value for a null, a NaN, or a value below or above the scale. Scale Bin edges LinearScale Equal-width bins LogarithmicScale Spaced logarithmically ExponentialScale Spaced exponentially MonomialScale Bin widths that grow as a power law IdentityScale One bin per integer from tabsdatak.dataquality import InBins, LinearScale, ScaleCategorizer, Select # splits amount into five equal-width bins between 0 and 10000 ScaleCategorizer([("amount", "amount_bin")], scale=LinearScale(0.0, 10000.0, bins=5), prefix="") # copies orders in the top bin, or above the scale, to large_orders Select(InBins(column_name="amount_bin", bins={5, "overflow"}), to_table="large_orders") Bins are numbered from 1. A scale created with use_bin_zero=True gives its minimum value a bin 0 of its own.

Criteria select the rows that the Filter, Select, and Fail operators act on. Criteria Selects rows where AllOk() Every boolean classifier passes AnyFailed() At least one boolean classifier fails InBins(column_name, bins) A categorizer's bin is one of bins NotInBins(column_name, bins) A categorizer's bin is not one of bins AllOk and AnyFailed treat a null or NaN verdict as a failure, unless none_is_ok=True or nan_is_ok=True is set. InBins and NotInBins accept bin numbers from 0 to 100 and the special bins "none", "nan", "underflow", and "overflow".

Operator Effect Enrich() Adds each classifier's verdict column to the Table, or to to_table. No rows are removed. Summary() Writes a summary with one row per classifier, holding its verdict counts or bin counts, to a Table named <table>_dq_summary, or to table. Filter(criteria) Removes the selected rows. They are discarded, or written to to_table. Select(criteria, to_table) Copies the selected rows to to_table, leaving the Table unchanged. Fail(criteria, threshold) Fails the Transaction when the number of selected rows reaches the threshold. Filter and Select take include_quality_columns to choose which verdict columns are carried into to_table: "none" (the default), "criteria", or "all". The checked Table never carries them.

Fail takes a threshold of rows, as a count or as a percentage of the Table: from tabsdatak.dataquality import AnyFailed, Fail, PercentThreshold, RowCountThreshold # fails as soon as one row fails a rule Fail(criteria=AnyFailed(), threshold=RowCountThreshold(1)) # fails when a twentieth of the table fails a rule Fail(criteria=AnyFailed(), threshold=PercentThreshold(5)) A failed Transaction commits none of its Tables.

Tags scope an operator to some of a check's classifiers. An operator with tags applies only to the classifiers that carry a matching tag, and an operator without tags applies to all of them. from tabsdatak.dataquality import ( AnyFailed, DataQuality, Fail, Filter, IsNotNull, Matches, RowCountThreshold, ) DataQuality( table="customers", classifiers=[ IsNotNull(["customer_id"], tags=["critical"]), Matches(["email"], pattern=r"^[^@]+@[^@]+$", tags=["cleanup"]), ], operators=[ # fails the transaction on a missing key Fail(criteria=AnyFailed(tags=["critical"]), threshold=RowCountThreshold(1)), # moves rows with a malformed email aside without failing Filter(AnyFailed(tags=["cleanup"]), to_table="customers_bad_email"), ], )

A Summary records how a Table's data quality looked in one Transaction. Trends keep that history: every time the check runs, its summary is folded into a trend Table that holds the recent runs one by one, plus weekly and monthly totals that reach further back. Reading the trend Table shows whether a rule fails more or less often over time, without keeping every version of the summary. Trends are off by default. Turn them on by passing Trends() to the trends argument of Summary: from tabsdatak.api import transformer, TableFrameSpec from tabsdatak.dataquality import ( DataQuality, IsBetween, IsIn, IsNotNull, Summary, Trends, ) @transformer( input_tables=["raw_orders"], output_tables=["orders"], on_tables=[ DataQuality( table="orders", classifiers=[ IsNotNull(["order_id"]), IsBetween(["amount"], min_val=0, max_val=10000), IsIn(["status"], values={"open", "shipped", "cancelled"}), ], operators=[Summary(trends=Trends())], ), ], ) def clean_orders(raw_orders: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return raw_orders.unique() Each run of clean_orders writes orders_dq_summary as before, and Tabsdata then folds that summary into orders_dq_summary_trends. The classifiers run while the data is written, in the same execution of the Function. Tabsdata does not read the Table again afterwards to compute the summary or the trend, so there is no separate quality job and no second pass over the data. The summary and trend Tables are Tabsdata Tables, versioned like any other. Every execution creates a new version of both, so the summary and the trend of any past execution can be read as they were at that point. See Data Quality for the classifiers and operators a check is built from.

The Tabsdata UI recognizes data quality Tables and shows them without any setup. A Table that has data quality checks is marked with a Q next to its name, in the Table list and in the execution plan graph. The data quality summary of the leads Table for one execution, opened from the execution plan graph: 100 rows checked, 10 checks, grouped by column. Each check shows its pass rate and how many rows failed or were null, and the lowest pass rate is called out at the top. The Data Quality Trends tab of the leads Table, with its trend chart expanded: the pass rate of every classifier, execution by execution. Hovering over an execution shows all the pass rates at that point. A Table's data quality shows in two places: The Table's page. A Table with a summary has a Data Quality Summaries tab, and a Table with a trend has a Data Quality Trends tab. Each tab lists the Table's summary or trend Tables; select one to chart it. The execution plan graph. Right-click a Table and open Data Quality > Data Quality Summary or Data Quality Trend to see the summary or trend as it was written by that execution. The trend chart, titled Pass rate by classifier, plots pass_pct for every classifier: Runs, Weeks, and Months switch between the run, week, and month rows of the trend Table. Buckets are in UTC, and weeks start on Monday. The legend button shows or hides individual classifiers, and the expand button opens a larger chart. On the Data Quality Trends tab, a trend Table can be pinned, so that its chart stays on the board while other trend Tables are selected.

documents.t: Trends configures the trend Table: its name and how long each tier keeps its rows. from tabsdatak.dataquality import Summary, Trends Summary(trends=Trends()) Summary(trends=Trends(table="orders_quality_history", days=14, weeks=26, months=36)) Summary(trends=Trends(days=7, weeks=13, months=0)) The first keeps the default retention, the second names the Table and keeps longer history, and the third keeps no month tier.

table​ The Table the trend is written to, as a valid table name. Defaults to None, which writes to <target>_dq_summary_trends, where <target> is the Table the DataQuality check runs on. The default name does not follow Summary(table=...): a summary written to orders_quality still gets its trend in orders_dq_summary_trends unless table is set. A name given here is used as is, with no suffix added. The trend Table is created in the same collection as the Function. days​ How many days a run is kept as its own row, as a non-negative integer. Defaults to 7. A run counts towards its week and month from its first execution, so expiring its run row does not remove it from the coarser tiers. 0 keeps no run rows. weeks​ How many weeks a week row is kept, counted from the Monday that starts it, as a non-negative integer. Defaults to 12, which keeps the current week and the 11 before it. 0 keeps no week rows. months​ How many months a month row is kept, counted from the 1st of the month, as a non-negative integer. Defaults to 24, which keeps the current month and the 23 before it. 0 keeps no month rows. At least one of days, weeks, and months must be greater than zero. To keep no trend, leave trends unset.

The trend Table holds four kinds of rows, told apart by the grain column: grain One row per bucket holds run classifier and run The time of the run week classifier and week Monday 00:00 UTC of the week month classifier and month The 1st of the month, 00:00 UTC folded Transaction already counted The time of the run The tiers overlap. A run is added to its week and its month as soon as it happens, not when its run row expires, so the current week row already includes the runs that are still listed one by one, and a month row includes every run of that month. Each tier expires on its own: a week that falls out of the weeks window is still counted in its month row. Weeks and months are bucketed independently, so a week that crosses into a new month is one week row while its runs count towards two month rows. Adding week rows together does not give a month row.

Retention is measured against the newest run folded into the Table, not against the wall clock. With the defaults, after a run on a given day the Table holds: a run row for each run in the 7 days before it a week row for that week and each of the 11 weeks before it a month row for that month and each of the 23 months before it Rows only expire when the trend is updated, so a Table whose check stops running keeps its last rows as they were.

Each folded row records one Transaction whose results the week and month rows already include. It carries the Transaction ID and the time of the run, and no counts. When a summary arrives for a Transaction that has a folded row, for example because the Transaction was recovered, it is not counted a second time. Summaries that arrive out of order are still counted once each. A folded row is kept for as long as the week or month tier could still be holding that run. When both weeks and months are 0, no folded rows are kept.

Column Type Description grain string run, week, month, or folded. bucket datetime (UTC) The run time for run and folded rows, the Monday that starts the week for week rows, and the 1st of the month for month rows. classifier string The verdict column the counts belong to, as in the summary, for example @td.dq.order_id_is_not_null or the name given in a (column, verdict_column) tuple with its prefix. Null on folded rows. runs int64 1 on a run row; the number of runs in the bucket on week and month rows. Null on folded rows. passed int64 Rows that passed the classifier. failed int64 Rows that failed the classifier. nulls int64 Rows with a null verdict. nans int64 Rows with a NaN verdict. pass_pct float64 passed * 100 / (passed + failed). Null and NaN verdicts are left out. Null when passed + failed is 0, and on folded rows. txn string The Transaction ID on run and folded rows. Null on week and month rows. folded_through datetime (UTC) The time of the newest run folded so far. Every row of a version holds the same value. On week and month rows, passed, failed, nulls, and nans are summed over the runs in the bucket, so pass_pct is the share of passing rows across the whole bucket, not an average of the runs' percentages. Like every Tabsdata Table, the trend Table also carries the $td. system columns. Only boolean classifiers are tracked. ScaleCategorizer results appear in the summary but not in the trend Table, and a summary with only categorizers adds no rows to its trend Table. Tags on Summary apply as usual: the trend tracks the classifiers the summary includes.

Registering a Function that declares Summary(trends=Trends(...)) also registers a second Function, the trend Function. The trend Function: is named after the trend Table with _trend appended, for example orders_dq_summary_trends_trend reads the latest summary and the latest version of the trend Table, and writes a new version of the trend Table runs in the same execution as the parent Function, after the summary is written is registered even in a collection that does not otherwise accept transformers Each run writes a new version of the whole trend Table: the previous version is read back, the new summary is merged in, and the rows that fell out of their tier's window are dropped. Earlier versions of the trend Table stay available like any other Table's. The trend Table is linked to the Table the check runs on, not to the summary, and its data versions report that Table as their parent.
documents.s: How the trend Table is maintained

documents.t: The trend Function belongs to the Function that declares the Summary, its parent, and follows it: Updating the parent Function with the same declaration keeps the same trend Function. Changing days, weeks, or months keeps its name. Renaming the trend Table, through table, replaces the trend Function with one named after the new Table. Adding trends to an existing Summary registers a trend Function on the next update. Removing trends, or the whole DataQuality check, deletes the trend Function. The trend Table is kept, frozen, with its history. Deleting the parent Function deletes the trend Function, and leaves their Tables frozen. Registering the parent Function again with tdk fn register --reuse-tables takes the frozen Tables back, history included. Disabling or enabling the parent Function does the same to the trend Function. Moving the check to another Table of the same Function keeps the summary and trend Tables and links them to the new Table. No longer producing the Table the check runs on freezes that Table, its summary, and its trend Table. Deleting the frozen Table also deletes the summary and trend Tables derived from it. The trend Function cannot be managed directly. Updating, patching, deleting, enabling, disabling, or triggering it by name is refused with: Function '<name>' is a child function managed by its parent; it cannot be updated, patched, deleted, enabled or triggered directly Make the change on the parent Function instead.

A sales operations team publishes the Salesforce Lead Lifetime report once a week and wants to know which data entry problems are getting better. The publisher checks every run and keeps a trend: from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, publisher from tabsdatak.conn.salesforce import SalesforceReportSrc from tabsdatak.dataquality import ( DataQuality, HasLength, IsBetween, IsIn, IsNotIn, IsNotNull, IsPositive, Matches, Summary, Trends, ) @publisher( source=SalesforceReportSrc(reports=["Lead Lifetime Report"], find_report_by="name"), output_tables=["leads"], on_tables=[ DataQuality( table="leads", classifiers=[ IsNotNull([("EMAIL", "email_present")]), Matches([("EMAIL", "email_valid")], pattern=r"^[^@]+@[^@]+\.[A-Za-z]{2,}$"), IsNotNull([("LEAD_SOURCE", "lead_source_present")]), IsNotIn([("COMPANY", "company_provided")], values={"[not provided]", "N/A", "Unknown"}), IsIn([("RATING", "rating_valid")], values={"Hot", "Warm", "Cold"}), IsBetween([("EMPLOYEES", "employees_in_range")], min_val=1, max_val=10_000), HasLength([("LAST_NAME", "last_name_valid")], min_len=2, max_len=80), IsPositive([("ANNUAL_REVENUE", "revenue_positive")]), ], operators=[Summary(trends=Trends(days=35))], ) ], ) def leads_report(leads: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return leads The report runs once a week, so with the default days=7 only the latest run would keep a row of its own. days=35 keeps the last five runs individually. The trend lands in leads_dq_summary_trends, with one classifier per verdict column: @td.dq.email_present, @td.dq.email_valid, and so on. After a few weeks, the trend separates the problems that are being fixed, such as missing emails once the web form makes the field required, from those that hold steady and those that come and go with list imports. For example, the month row for August 2026 might read: grain bucket classifier runs passed failed pass_pct month 2026-08-01 00:00:00 UTC @td.dq.email_present 4 362 38 90.5
documents.s: Tracking a source report run by run

documents.t: Use tdk table data with --sql to look at one tier: tdk table data --coll sales --name leads_dq_summary_trends --sql "SELECT bucket, classifier, runs, failed, pass_pct FROM leads_dq_summary_trends WHERE grain = 'week' ORDER BY classifier, bucket" --print folded_through shows which run the trend has caught up to. The trend Function commits in the same Transaction as the summary, so a committed summary version always has its trend version next to it.

A transformer can take the trend Table as an input like any other Table, for example to publish a weekly quality scorecard for a dashboard: from tabsdatak.api import TableFrameSpec, transformer from tabsdatak.tableframe.functions import col @transformer( input_tables=["sales/leads_dq_summary_trends"], output_tables=["leads_weekly_quality"], ) def leads_weekly_quality(trends: TableFrameSpec) -> TableFrameSpec: return trends.filter(col("grain") == "week").select( "bucket", "classifier", "runs", "passed", "failed", "pass_pct" ) Each new version of the trend Table triggers the transformer, so the scorecard is refreshed after every run of the report.

A pipeline that runs every few minutes produces many run rows. Keeping a day of runs and a quarter of weeks, with no month tier, bounds the Table's size: from tabsdatak.dataquality import Summary, Trends Summary(trends=Trends(days=1, weeks=13, months=0))

Trends are only maintained for boolean classifiers. Categorizer results stay in the summary Table. Retention values are whole numbers of days, weeks, or months, 0 or greater. A negative value, a float, a string, or a boolean is refused with error DQC_32, as is an invalid table name. Setting days, weeks, and months all to 0 is refused with error DQC_33. Leave trends unset to keep no trend. Every Table a check produces must have a unique name, and that includes trend Tables. Two Summary operators with trends on the same check need different table names for their trends, or registration fails with error DQPE_4. Week and month buckets are always in UTC; weeks start on Monday and months on the 1st. There is no option to bucket in another time zone. A tier that was disabled and is later enabled starts from the runs that follow; it is not filled in from older run rows. The trend Function is managed through the Function that declares the Summary. It cannot be triggered, updated, or deleted on its own.

Grok parses lines of text, such as the lines of a log file, into typed columns. The grok method of a TableFrame matches a Grok pattern against a string column and appends one column for each capture listed in a schema. Grok is usually applied in the Publisher that reads the log file, so the Table it writes is already structured. Because grok is a TableFrame method, it can also be used in a Transformer on a Table that holds raw text. For a full walkthrough that reads a log file and publishes the parsed rows, see Publish data from log files with Grok.

grok takes three arguments: The name of the string column to parse, or an expression that resolves to one A Grok pattern whose named captures become the new columns A schema that maps each capture name to a ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok import ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes import String, Int32, Int64 PATTERN = ( r"%{IPV4:client_ip} " r"%{USER:ident} " r"%{USER:auth} " r"\[%{HTTPDATE:timestamp}\] " r'"%{WORD:method} ' r'%{URIPATHPARAM:request} ' r'HTTP/%{NUMBER:http_version}" ' r"%{INT:response_code} %{INT:bytes}" ) SCHEMA = { "client_ip": ColumnDefinition("ip_address", String), "method": ColumnDefinition("http_method", String), "response_code": ColumnDefinition("status_code", Int32), "bytes": ColumnDefinition("response_bytes", Int64), "timestamp": ColumnDefinition("request_time", String), } parsed = lines.grok("column_1", PATTERN, SCHEMA) lines column_1 203.0.113.10 - - [10/Oct/2026:13:55:01 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 512 not a log line 2 rows parsed column_1str ip_addressstr http_methodstr status_codei32 response_bytesi64 request_timestr 203.0.113.10 - - [10/Oct/2026:13:55:01 +0000] "GET /index.html HTTP/1.1" 200 512 203.0.113.10 GET 200 512 10/Oct/2026:13:55:01 +0000 not a log line null null null null null 2 rows The result keeps every existing column and follows these rules: One column is added for each entry in the schema, in schema order. Captures that are not in the schema are not added. The pattern above captures ident, auth, request, and http_version, but none of them become columns. The captured text is cast to the dtype in the capture's ColumnDefinition. A row whose text does not match the pattern gets null in every new column, so a malformed line never fails the Function.

A capture is written as %{PATTERN:capture}, where PATTERN is a predefined pattern name and capture is the name the schema refers to. Text between captures must match literally, so characters that have a meaning in regular expressions, such as [ and ], are escaped with a backslash. The full capture syntax is %{name:alias:extract:definition}: name: a predefined pattern name, such as IPV4, WORD, or INT alias: the capture name extract: reserved for future use definition: a regular expression, required when no predefined name is given Tabsdata includes 320 predefined patterns from the Elasticsearch Grok pattern library. Commonly used patterns for log files include: Pattern Matches IPV4 An IPv4 address WORD A single word INT An integer NUMBER An integer or decimal number TIMESTAMP_ISO8601 An ISO 8601 timestamp HTTPDATE A timestamp in web server access log format LOGLEVEL A log level, such as INFO or ERROR UUID A UUID URI A URI DATA Any text, matching as little as possible GREEDYDATA Any text, matching as much as possible COMBINEDAPACHELOG A full Apache combined log line SYSLOGBASE The header of a syslog line

The schema is a dictionary keyed by capture name. Each value is a ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok with two fields: name: the name of the new column. None keeps the capture name, and any other value renames the column. dtype: the data type the captured text is cast to, from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes. Defaults to String. from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok import ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes import String PATTERN = r"%{TIMESTAMP_ISO8601:ts} %{LOGLEVEL:level} %{WORD:service}: %{GREEDYDATA:message}" SCHEMA = { "ts": ColumnDefinition(None, String), "level": ColumnDefinition("level", String), "service": ColumnDefinition("service", String), "message": ColumnDefinition("message", String), }

When a pattern uses the same capture name more than once, each repeat is numbered: the first keeps the name, and later ones get a [1], [2], … suffix. The schema refers to repeats by those numbered names. from tabsdatak.tableframe.grok import ColumnDefinition from tabsdatak.tableframe.datatypes import String, Int64 PATTERN = r"%{WORD:city}-%{INT:year} to %{WORD:city}-%{INT:year}" SCHEMA = { "city": ColumnDefinition("from_city", String), "city[1]": ColumnDefinition("to_city", String), "year[1]": ColumnDefinition("to_year", Int64), } The grok_fields helper lists the capture names a pattern produces, which is useful for building the schema of a long pattern: from tabsdata.expansions.tableframe.features.grok.engine import grok_fields grok_fields(r"%{WORD:city}-%{INT:year} to %{WORD:city}-%{INT:year}") # ['city', 'city[1]', 'year', 'year[1]']

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) Server lets an external AI agent work with your Tabsdata Server. An agent can inspect resources, write and register Functions, query Tables, and investigate failed executions. Claude Code and Codex connect to it through the tabsdata-agent package. The MCP Server and Tabby share the same tools. Tabby is the chat in the Tabsdata UI; MCP makes those tools available to the agent you use in your terminal or editor.

The MCP Server gives the agent access to: Resources: Projects, Groups, Collections, Connections, Functions, and Tables. Data: Table schemas, data versions, and queries against published data. Executions: Execution Plans, Transactions, Function Runs, and logs for diagnosing failures. Reference: SDK documentation, connector information, and code examples for writing Functions. Skills: instructions for tasks such as creating a data flow or fixing an execution. The agent searches for the tools and skills it needs as it works. For example, you can ask it to list the Tables in a Collection, inspect a failed Function Run, or build a Publisher from a database table.

Your agent starts a local MCP proxy with: python -m tabsdatak.ag.mcp - The trailing - selects standard input and output as the transport between the agent and the proxy. This command belongs in the agent's MCP configuration. See Connect to MCP for the installation commands. The proxy reads the Server address and session saved by tdk login, then forwards requests to the Server's /ai-agent/proxy/mcp endpoint over HTTP. The agent uses your Tabsdata session and has your permissions. The proxy reads the session again on each request. If your login expires or you switch Servers, run tdk login again. The next request uses the new session without restarting the proxy.

The MCP Server runs in the same AI agent service as Tabby, on port 2459 by default. That service must be running before an external agent can use its tools. An Anthropic or OpenAI API key must be set when the Server is created for the AI agent service to start. MCP itself does not need a valid LLM key, so a placeholder is sufficient when only using an external agent. Tabby requires a valid key. See Tabby requirements for setting or changing it.

If the agent cannot reach Tabsdata, check that the Server and its AI agent service are running. If the session is no longer valid, log in again and retry the request. If Python cannot find tabsdatak.ag.mcp, install tabsdata-agent in the environment used by the agent's MCP command.

Credentials used by Publisher and Subscriber Functions are stored in Connections. Connections are credential stores that are attached to collections, which enable the function inside the collection to use the credentials. To register a connection into Tabsdata, the user must generate a .yaml connection document template through the tdk connection template cli command and fill in the required credentials. Once the document is completed, it must be attached to a collection through the tdk collection create or tdk collection update cli command. During connection registration, Tabsdata dehydrates the Connection document by extracting its credentials into a separate secret store and replacing them in the stored Connection with references to those secrets. Once stored, credentials are only made available to a Function when it runs. In fact, once credentials are in Tabsdata, there is no way to read them out of the system. This is by design, ensuring your secrets are always secure. When creating workflows through MCP, it is important to remember that you must provide your credentials to your LLM in order for it to pass those credentials into Tabsdata. It is important to understand the security implications of doing so. There are several ways to pass secrets to an LLM for creating connections. COLLECTIONWRITTEN INTOREGISTERED INTOUSED BYpasswordconnection documentConnectionFunction

The most secure option is to create the Connection outside of the agent. You can ask the agent to generate a Connection template, then add the credentials yourself, and register the Connection with Tabsdata using the `tdk connection create` or tdk connection update` CLI command. The agent can then create or register Functions against the Collection without ever accessing the credentials required. This keeps the credentials out of the agent's context and session history.

Connection templates can reference credentials using $secret:<VARIABLE>. When working through an agent, the environment variable must be available to both the process running the LLM and the Tabsdata server. This means the variable must be set in the shell environment before both processes are started. This avoids placing the credential directly in the agent prompt, but still gives the agent process access to it. Environment variables may also be visible to other processes running in the same environment. For these reasons, environment variables are better suited for development and testing than for long-lived production credentials. Adding or updating secrets also requires restarting both the agent and the Tabsdata server with the updated shell environment. warning Storing credentials in environment variables does not prevent the agent from accessing their values. However, it allows the agent to pass the environment variable name as a literal to the Tabsdata server, which can then resolve the value server-side. This reduces the likelihood of the secret being captured in the agent's transcript.

You can also provide credentials directly to the agent and have it create the Connection for you. This is the simplest option, but the credential passes through the agent's context and may be stored in its session history. Credentials provided this way may be at increased risk for exposure.
documents.s: Provide Credentials Directly to the Agent

documents.t: In scenarios where the agent is requesting multiple points of data, or in sessions where providing credentials directly inline requires pasting the same content multiple times, you can pass all relevant data into a .txt file and pass the path to the agent during your session warning Putting credentials in a file and asking an agent to read that file does not prevent the agent from accessing them. Once the agent reads the file, the credentials have passed through the agent just as if they were provided directly.

Tabby is the built-in Tabsdata agent, opened from the Tabby page of the User Interface. Tabby answers questions about the resources on a Tabsdata Server and, when the Server allows it, creates and changes them on request. note Tabby is an AI feature and requires an LLM API key, from Anthropic or OpenAI, provided when the Server is created. See Requirements for the flags and for adding a key to an existing Server. AITabby Did any execution plans fail in customer_management? No. The 10 most recent execution plans in customer_management all finished, and each one committed 5 function runs with no errors. The three latest: Execution plan Triggered by Status Duration ep20260924-14 salesforce/ingest_opportunities Finished 11s ep20260924-13 salesforce/ingest_leads Finished 12s ep20260924-12 salesforce/ingest_customers Finished 12s Each plan runs the Salesforce ingest for one entity, then its bronze, silver, and gold transformers and the Snowflake load. anthropic claude-sonnet-4-6 Ask anything about your data flows… (⌘K) ↑ The UI demo includes the Tabby page. Messages cannot be sent from the demo. Open Tabby in the UI demo

Tabby runs in the Server's AI agent service, on port 2459 by default, and requires an Anthropic or OpenAI API key. When no key is configured, the Server starts without the AI agent service and Tabby is unavailable. The key is set when the instance is created, with --config anthropic-key=… or --config openai-key=…: tdkserver quickstart --config anthropic-key=env:ANTHROPIC_API_KEY To add or change the key on an existing instance, download the instance's config, set api_key under ai_providers.anthropic or ai_providers.openai in aiagent.yaml, and apply the change: tdkserver config get --with-secrets tdkserver config put --apply The MCP Server runs in the same AI agent service. A key must be configured for the service to start, but a placeholder is sufficient when only using an external agent. Tabby requires a valid key.

Open Tabby from the side navigation, or press ⌘K from any page to ask Tabby about the page you are viewing. A new chat offers four starting prompts: Set up a data flow Connect to an external system Check executions health Show me what Tabsdata can do Other pages suggest prompts for what they show. A Collection page, for example, suggests listing its Functions, listing its Tables, and creating a Publisher.

Commands are typed into the message box. Command Description /help Show available commands /new Start a new conversation /clear Clear the current conversation /export Export the conversation as Markdown /models List available providers and models /provider <name> Switch AI provider /model <name> Switch to a specific model, by full or partial name /health Show agent health and status /pop [name] Open resources from the conversation in new tabs, or one resource by name The provider and model can also be switched from the selector above the message box.

Chats are stored on the Server and can be continued later. From a chat, you can: Search the chat's messages Export the chat as Markdown Stop a response while it is being generated Retry a response that failed

Tabby can write a custom connector for a system that Tabsdata does not support natively. Tabby's reference includes the connector interface in tabsdatak.spi, and every connector installed on the Server, including custom ones, is part of what Tabby knows. Installing the connector remains a manual step. See Custom Connectors.
Whether Tabby can create, change, or delete resources is set by allow_writes in the Server's aiagent.yaml config.

The Tabsdata User Interface (UI) is a web interface for inspecting and managing the resources within a Tabsdata Server. When running Tabsdata locally, the UI is available at http://localhost:2457, where 2457 is the Server's default public port. Sign in using the same username and password used with the tdk CLI. The UI demo provides a read-only Tabsdata Server with three Projects and existing execution history. Actions that create, modify, trigger, or delete resources are disabled. Explore the UI

The Overview page summarizes activity across every Project in the Server. For each Project, the page shows: Tables committed Rows committed Running Executions Warnings Errors Activity can be viewed across six time ranges.

The Projects page shows activity for the selected Project, including data that is currently in flight and data that has already been committed. The page also includes a graph of committed data over time. From the UI, you can: Create Projects Share Projects Switch the currently selected Project Most pages in the UI are scoped to the selected Project. Use the Project selector in the side panel to switch between Projects.

The Collections page lists the Collections within the selected Project. Opening a Collection shows its: Functions Tables Connection configuration Sensitive credentials stored in a Connection are hidden from the UI. From the UI, you can also: Create, edit, and delete Collections Grant a Collection access to Tables in another Collection Remove previously granted access

Opening a Function shows the code registered with Tabsdata and its version history. Function versions are retained so you can inspect previous versions, including the version used for a particular Function Run. From the UI, you can: Trigger a Function Delete a Function Editing a Function's code is performed using tdk rather than through the UI.

Opening a Table shows its schema, sample rows, and version history. Each Table version includes the Execution that wrote it, allowing changes in the Table to be traced back to the Execution that produced them. The Table page also includes Run SQL query, which lets you edit and run a SQL query against the Table's sample data. From the UI, you can also delete a Table.

The Executions page shows the Execution Plans created within the selected Project. Execution Plans are separated into: Active Issues Finished Opening an Execution Plan shows a graph of its execution flow and provides access to the Transactions, Function Runs, and Workers created as part of the Execution. Transactions, Function Runs, and Workers can each be filtered by status.

Opening a Worker provides access to the logs produced while it was running. Worker logs can be: Viewed in the UI Viewed in their raw form Downloaded When a Function Run fails, its Worker logs contain the output and errors produced during execution.

The Executions area also shows the triggers configured for the Project, including: Cron Triggers Stream Sources This lets you inspect both what causes Functions to run and the Execution Plans created when they run.
The Search page searches for resources across the Tabsdata Server. Use Search to locate a resource without navigating through its Project and Collection.

Tabby is the built-in Tabsdata agent for interacting with and inspecting a Tabsdata Server. See Tabby for setup, commands, and an example chat. Tabby requires an Anthropic or OpenAI API key to be configured on the Server. From Tabby, you can: Start a new chat Continue existing chats Stop a response while it is being generated Search previous messages Export a chat as Markdown Use page-specific suggested prompts Run a Server health check Suggested prompts depend on the page you are viewing. For example, a Collection page may include prompts for listing Functions or creating a Publisher. The Run health check action generates an AI-written report about the current health of the Server.

The Security page manages users, roles, and permissions for the Tabsdata Server. From the UI, you can: Create, edit, and delete users Create and delete roles Add users to roles Remove users from roles Grant permissions Remove permissions
The System page shows the status and runtime information for the Tabsdata Server.

The Account page shows information about the currently signed-in user. From the UI, you can also: Change your password Log out Switch between light and dark themes Pin resources to the side panel Clear pinned resources The Server's SSL certificate can also be downloaded from the login page.

A custom connector allows Tabsdata to connect to external systems that are not officially supported by the current suite of Tabsdata connectors. Custom Connectors are python packages that can be coded by hand or by AI agents connected through Tabsdata's MCP Server.

This guide builds a SQLite connector as an example. Create a directory named sqlite_connector with the following files. The Python package lives in src/tabsdata_sqlite. ⌄sqlite_connector pyproject.toml ⌄src ⌄tabsdata_sqlite error.py __init__.py _plugin.py pyproject.toml defines the package, dependencies, and entry points Tabsdata uses to discover the connector. error.py defines errors for invalid configuration and failed reads or writes. __init__.py defines the connection and function configuration classes users import. _plugin.py implements the read and write logic and registers the connector with Tabsdata. tip Download the connector template using the button at the top right of the file tree, or copy the files below. The highlighted lines are the main parts you would change when adapting this example to another system.

pyproject.toml defines the package metadata, Python dependencies, and entry points Tabsdata uses to load the connector. When adapting this file: Set the package name, version, and description. Add any Python packages the connector needs to dependencies. Define one entry point for each source or destination the package provides. pyproject.toml [build-system] requires = ["setuptools>=69"] build-backend = "setuptools.build_meta" [project] name = "tabsdata-conn-sqlite" version = "0.1.0" description = "Tabsdata source and destination connector for SQLite databases." requires-python = ">=3.12" dependencies = [ "tabsdata>=2.1,<2.2", ] [tool.setuptools.packages.find] where = ["src"] [project.entry-points."tabsdatak.connectors"] src_sqlite = "tabsdata_sqlite._plugin:SQLITE_SRC" dest_sqlite = "tabsdata_sqlite._plugin:SQLITE_DEST"

error.py defines the different errors that can occur during connector usage. SQLITE_1 through SQLITE_4 are assigned to the configuration classes in __init__.py and report invalid connection or function settings. SQLITE_1 when the source connection document fails validation (invalid credentials) SQLITE_1 when the destination connection document fails validation (invalid credentials) SQLITE_3 when the source connector fails validation (missing/invalid arguments provided) SQLITE_4 when the destination connector fails validation (missing/invalid arguments provided) You can define additional error codes in error.py and raise them in _plugin.py to handle failures during execution. SQLITE_5 when a query fails. SQLITE_6 when the number of returned tables does not match the configured destination tables. SQLITE_7 when a write fails. Message placeholders such as {table} are filled when .exception() is called. error.py from tabsdatak.conn.common.error import ConnException, ConnInitException from tabsdatak.error import ErrorCode, ErrorDef class SqliteRuntimeException(ConnException): """A SQLite read or write failed.""" class SqliteErrorCode(ErrorCode): SQLITE_1 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteSrcConn validation failed") SQLITE_2 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteDestConn validation failed") SQLITE_3 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteSrc validation failed") SQLITE_4 = ErrorDef(ConnInitException, "SqliteDest validation failed") SQLITE_5 = ErrorDef(SqliteRuntimeException, "SQLite query {index} failed") SQLITE_6 = ErrorDef( SqliteRuntimeException, "SQLite received {slots} table(s) for {tables} target table(s)", ) SQLITE_7 = ErrorDef(SqliteRuntimeException, "SQLite write to {table} failed")

__init__.py defines the classes users import from tabsdata_sqlite and what arguments these classes can accept. SqliteSrcConn: Connection Document for Source Connectors SqliteSrc: Source Connector SqliteDestConn: Connection for Destination Connectors SqliteDest: Destination Connector Within each class, define the configuration fields and their types. Pass the appropriate validation error code as the first argument to the @_api.dataclass decorator. @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_1, kw_only=True) class SqliteSrcConn(Conn): """Connection to the SQLite database a publisher reads.""" path: StrOrSecretSpec tip The SqlLiteSrcConn above is configured to accept a single path argument as either a string or a secret. If this condition is not met, it throws the SQLite_1 error code. __init__.py from typing import Annotated, Literal from pydantic import StringConstraints import tabsdatak._api as _api from tabsdatak.api import Dest, Secret, Src, StrOrSecretSpec from tabsdatak.spi import Conn from tabsdata_sqlite.error import SqliteErrorCode TableName = Annotated[str, StringConstraints(pattern=r"^[A-Za-z_][A-Za-z0-9_]*$")] def resolve(spec: StrOrSecretSpec) -> str: return spec.value() if isinstance(spec, Secret) else spec @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_1, kw_only=True) class SqliteSrcConn(Conn): """Connection to the SQLite database a publisher reads.""" path: StrOrSecretSpec @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_2, kw_only=True) class SqliteDestConn(Conn): """Connection to the SQLite database a subscriber writes.""" path: StrOrSecretSpec @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_3, kw_only=True) class SqliteSrc(Src): """Queries a publisher runs against SQLite.""" queries: list[str] @_api.dataclass(SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_4, kw_only=True) class SqliteDest(Dest): """SQLite tables that receive a subscriber's returned data.""" tables: list[TableName] if_table_exists: Literal["append", "replace"] = "replace" Under this configuration, the source connection defines where Tabsdata connects the source connector defines what query to read from the database the destination connection defines where Tabsdata connects the destination connector defines what Tabsdata tables are written into SQLite and whether to append or replace existing tables. During execution, Tabsdata passes both objects to the connector plugin. __init__.py · Connection class SqliteSrcConn(Conn): path: StrOrSecretSpec → conn-sqlite-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdata_sqlite:SqliteSrcConn spec: path: str:/data/shop.db __init__.py · Source class SqliteSrc(Src): queries: list[str] → pub_shop.py source=SqliteSrc( queries=[ "SELECT * FROM customers", "SELECT * FROM orders", ], )

_plugin.py contains the connector's runtime logic that uses the inputs defined in __init__.py SqliteSrcPlugin.read_in: Runs each query from the Publisher configuration. Writes each query result to a Parquet file in ctx.work_dir. Returns those files in the same order as src.queries. If a query fails, the plugin raises SQLITE_5 with the query index and original exception. SqliteDestPlugin.write_out: Checks that the number of returned table slots matches dest.tables. Matches each returned file to the destination table in the same position. Skips any None file reference. Reads each remaining Parquet file. Replaces or appends to the destination table based on dest.if_table_exists. _plugin.py import sqlite3 from pathlib import Path import polars as pl from tabsdatak.spi import ( DestContext, DestDef, DestPlugin, SrcDef, SrcPlugin, SrcPluginCtx, TableFileInput, TableFileSpec, TableMode, ) from tabsdata_sqlite import ( SqliteDest, SqliteDestConn, SqliteSrc, SqliteSrcConn, resolve, ) from tabsdata_sqlite.error import SqliteErrorCode def connect(conn: SqliteSrcConn | SqliteDestConn) -> sqlite3.Connection: return sqlite3.connect(resolve(conn.path)) class SqliteSrcPlugin(SrcPlugin[SqliteSrcConn, SqliteSrc]): def read_in( self, ctx: SrcPluginCtx, conn: SqliteSrcConn, src: SqliteSrc, ) -> list[list[TableFileInput]]: con = connect(conn) try: slots = [] for index, query in enumerate(src.queries): try: frame = pl.read_database(query, con) except Exception as e: raise SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_5.exception(cause=e, index=index) parquet = Path(ctx.work_dir) / f"{index}.parquet" frame.write_parquet(parquet) slots.append([TableFileInput(file=parquet)]) return slots finally: con.close() class SqliteDestPlugin(DestPlugin[SqliteDestConn, SqliteDest]): def write_out( self, ctx: DestContext, conn: SqliteDestConn, dest: SqliteDest, tables: list[TableFileSpec], ) -> None: if len(tables) != len(dest.tables): raise SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_6.exception( slots=len(tables), tables=len(dest.tables) ) con = connect(conn) try: with con: con.execute("BEGIN") for table, parquet in zip(dest.tables, tables): if parquet is None: continue try: frame = pl.read_parquet(parquet) columns = ", ".join( '"' + c.replace('"', '""') + '"' for c in frame.columns ) if dest.if_table_exists == "replace": con.execute(f'DROP TABLE IF EXISTS "{table}"') con.execute( f'CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS "{table}" ({columns})' ) marks = ", ".join("?" for _ in frame.columns) con.executemany( f'INSERT INTO "{table}" ({columns}) VALUES ({marks})', frame.iter_rows(), ) except Exception as e: raise SqliteErrorCode.SQLITE_7.exception(cause=e, table=table) finally: con.close() SQLITE_SRC = SrcDef( conn=SqliteSrcConn, type_="sqlite-sql-in", system="SQLite", src_version="v1", src=SqliteSrc, table_mode=TableMode.SINGLE, cardinality=lambda src: len(src.queries), plugin=SqliteSrcPlugin, explorer=None, icon=None, ) SQLITE_DEST = DestDef( conn=SqliteDestConn, type_="sqlite-sql-out", system="SQLite", dest_version="v1", dest=SqliteDest, cardinality=lambda dest: len(dest.tables), plugin=SqliteDestPlugin, explorer=None, icon=None, )

The connector package must be installed in two places: Wherever tdk runs locally, so Tabsdata can validate connections and register Functions. In the server's Function environment, so the connector is available when those Functions execute. Local Git PyPI Step 1Install the local package where tdk runs From the directory containing sqlite_connector, run: pip install ./sqlite_connector Step 2Add the local package to the server's Function environment requirements.txt tabsdata-conn-sqlite @ file:///absolute/path/to/sqlite_connector Step 3Update the server's Function environment tdkserver venv update \ --name fn \ --requirements requirements.txt danger This command overwrites Tabsdata's existing list of package requirements. Include every complementary package the environment still needs, not just the new one being added. Step 1Install the Git package where tdk runs Replace <org> and <repo> with the repository containing the connector: pip install "git+https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git#subdirectory=sqlite_connector" Step 2Add the Git package to the server's Function environment requirements.txt tabsdata-conn-sqlite @ git+https://github.com/<org>/<repo>.git#subdirectory=sqlite_connector Step 3Update the server's Function environment After tdkserver quickstart has created the instance, update its fn environment to include the package. tdkserver venv update \ --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE> \ --name fn \ --requirements requirements.txt danger This command overwrites Tabsdata's existing list of package requirements. Include every complementary package the environment still needs, not just the new one being added. Step 1Install the published package where tdk runs After publishing the connector to PyPI, install its package: pip install tabsdata-conn-sqlite==0.1.0 Step 2Add the published package to the server's Function environment requirements.txt tabsdata-conn-sqlite==0.1.0 Step 3Update the server's Function environment After tdkserver quickstart has created the instance, update its fn environment to include the package. tdkserver venv update \ --instance <TABSDATA_INSTANCE> \ --name fn \ --requirements requirements.txt danger This command overwrites Tabsdata's existing list of package requirements. Include every complementary package the environment still needs, not just the new one being added.

Step 4Generate the connection documents This works as long as SQLITE_SRC and SQLITE_DEST are registered through the tabsdatak.connectors entry points in pyproject.toml. tip Run tdk connection types to confirm that tdk can discover both custom connector types. Generate the appropriate connection template: Source Destination tdk connection template --type sqlite-sql-in --file conn-sqlite-in.yaml tdk connection template --type sqlite-sql-out --file conn-sqlite-out.yaml Step 5Fill out the connection documents The spec field contains the arguments defined in __init__.py. A completed document will look like this: Source Destination conn-sqlite-in.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdata_sqlite:SqliteSrcConn spec: path: str:/data/shop.db conn-sqlite-out.yaml kind: connectionDef apiVersion: '1.0' type: tabsdata_sqlite:SqliteDestConn spec: path: str:/data/warehouse.db Step 6Attach the connections to Collections New Collection Existing Collection Create a new collection and attach the filled-out connection document. Source Destination tdk collection create --name shop --group sources --conn-file conn-sqlite-in.yaml tdk collection create --name warehouse --group destinations --conn-file conn-sqlite-out.yaml Update an existing collection with the filled-out connection document. Source Destination tdk collection update --name shop --conn-file conn-sqlite-in.yaml tdk collection update --name warehouse --conn-file conn-sqlite-out.yaml
